Prior update: (**Student error detection** (`20260820_page_reports.sql`, §38.5 of the run plan): every wiki page gains a member-visible "Report an issue" control — `error` (no source; first verified report earns participation credit) vs `contradiction` (source required; staff verify and convert to a claimable amber gap, and the student's submission through the normal pipeline **counts toward the three required articles**). Prior update: **Sandy 3 §5.5 positive control reinterpreted, pre-data**: the registered check correlates predicted with experienced relative performance and calls failure a data-quality problem — but the Aptitude Suite is *built* to break that link (aim for the top 10%, live percentile for eight minutes), so a low r is what a working manipulation produces and the clause read success as failure. ColourMax was never a comparable reference: its prediction comes after feedback. Registered text untouched; Appendix C1 adds three diagnostics with thresholds fixed in advance, D1 (does the rating track the score actually shown) discriminating a broken slider from a working manipulation. On the pilot the control fails while all three pass. Amended with zero confirmatory participants enrolled, so it stays a prediction rather than an explanation. Prior update: **Featured media strip on the landing page**: the three flagged `media.json` entries (Future Mending Radio, Ten Percent Happier, Hidden Brain) render as a logo row below the hub cards, linking out to the episodes and through to `/lab/media`. Prior update: (**Sandy 3 analysis repo published private**, and a disclosure caught on the way: auditing the repo before its first push found `output/fix_verification.csv` carrying 20 platform profile UUIDs joined to participant scores — identifiable data in a versioned directory since 2026-08-11, missed because `data/` was carefully de-identified while `output/` read as “results”. Fixed at the artefact, the generator (so a re-run cannot reintroduce it) and the history (removed before first push — safe only because no clone existed). Rule worth carrying: no versioned file may hold a participant key, whatever directory it sits in, and the check belongs at first publication. Prior update: (**Sandy 3 pilot/confirmatory boundary enforced**: the preregistration always said the N=20 pilot would not be pooled with the registered sample, but nothing enforced it — the pilot participants sit in the same study id with the same Prolific id pattern, so the analysis pipeline's only cohort filter kept them all and a confirmatory run would have silently analysed them. Now bounded by enrolment date via `SANDY3_COHORT_START`, which a confirmatory run refuses to start without. Independent of the registration, the pilot ran the pre-2026-08-11 Aptitude Suite — Word Probe recalibration, partial credit, floored redemption score — so its percentiles were never on the same scale. Prior update: (**Aptitude Suite focus instrumentation** (`20260819_aptitude_suite_focus_events.sql`, `AptitudeSuite.jsx`): the suite now logs `session_start`, `game_end`, `task_focus` `{from,to}` and window blur/focus, closing the one measure Sandy Study 3's preregistration named but the platform never recorded — per-subtask time. Not a ColourMax analogue: ColourMax shows one image at a time so navigation is loggable, whereas all three Aptitude subtasks are on screen at once, so keyboard focus is the only observable signal and the measure stays exploratory by construction. Window listeners check `e.target === window`, since a bubbling element focus would otherwise read as the window returning and subtract an away-interval that never happened. R side reconstructs per-subtask dwell with blur intervals removed, checked by `_validate_apt_focus.R` (13 assertions). Found while cleaning up the test account: the analysis pipeline had **no `is_test` filter** despite the export carrying the flag and documenting it — now exclusion criterion 0, ahead of every behavioural criterion. Prior update: **The PSY240 red set closes, 12 of 12** — the gaps that must never be student work, because a wrong answer there would read as clinical instruction or a legal standard. All closed by direct-parse ingest in reporting register with an explicit not-clinical-instruction note: levodopa (the LEAP delayed-start result), flumazenil and benzodiazepine-misuse dependence management, deprescribing, the clinician's duty where the risk is to the patient (Ontario Form 1), the forensic paraphilias (Marshall & Kingston — expert agreement on sexual sadism at kappa 0.14, against the 0.9 standard psychometricians set for decisions like indefinite confinement), IED and criminal responsibility, R v Parks on the sleepwalking defence, CYFSA s.125 reporting duties, Tarasoff's interstate variation (76% of psychologists picked the wrong description of their own state's law), involuntary hospitalisation as prevention, and the Ontario HCCA / Consent-and-Capacity-Board pathway for ECT. Four source documents came from Norm, since the institutional hosts refuse automated fetch. Corpus 742 open, 133 green, 608 amber, 0 red. Prior update: **`_note` fields removed corpus-wide** (§26, `20260817_strip_intervention_note_fields.sql`): auditing all 48 intervention modules after the Graduation Day fix found 19 inert `_note` fields across 6 modules — and a **second** live defect of the same kind. The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise (`non-reactivity-phase2-day2`) declares *"all required before Next unlocks"* on each of its five steps while none sets `min_required`, and the renderer gates on `min_required ?? 1` — so the exercise whose entire content is the descending count of five, four, three, two, one was asking for one, one, one, one, one. Norm's call: strip the notes, then re-express the one real requirement among them as data — the grounding steps now set `min_required = count` ("if it asks for 3, let's get 3"), while the reappraisal "list all your automatic thoughts" steps keep `min_required: 1`, because there the count is a ceiling and forcing it would make participants invent thoughts they do not hold. The rule this leaves — **module JSON may contain data the renderer reads and nothing else**; a key the code never reads will be believed by every human who opens the file and honoured by nothing. Prior update: **Graduation Day's intention block is now gated, worded and verified live** (§26): the four follow-ups had shipped carrying their condition as a `_note` comment that nothing read, so every participant answered "When will you practice?" — including those who had just said they never would. They now sit behind an explicit yes/no, and the likelihood slider behind it, since gating the item changed *who is asked* and made its "Never" anchor unreachable; the span reads `Rarely · Occasionally · Sometimes · Often · Very often · Almost always` across six per-point labels. Two lessons worth carrying: **a condition written as a comment is not a condition**, and **changing who is asked a question changes what its anchors should say**. First full use of the `dev` → review → promote loop. Prior update: (**Check-in "Maybe later" fixed + formal-button policy**: the account merge passed a state-setter as `onComplete` to `/checkin`'s CheckinFlow, not realizing `onComplete` is a flow-control *override* — its presence suppresses the flow's own `navigate('/dashboard')`, so the suggestion step's "Maybe later" fired invisible state and went nowhere. Prior update: (**The last four weight-500 declarations, and a trial of three game icons**: `fontWeight="500"` on Still Water's wheel diagram survived every audit because the scanner looked for `font-weight:` in CSS and these were SVG presentation attributes — so `/brand` was claiming "zero occurrences site-wide" while four rendered as faux bold. Migrated to 600 (the spec's `body/600/12`); the claim is now true in CSS **and** in attributes, and `/brand` says which. Prior update: (**Study day in participant emails is a position, not a date** (§28 WP7): `{{study_day}}` resolved to `participant_schedule.study_day`, which counts *elapsed days since t0*, so a Graduation Day test email read "Study Day 39" for a session the protocol calls Day 28 — Phase 2 re-anchors to when a participant's fork resolves, so every day of midpoint delay pushes the number past the study's own day map. The page is now itself scale-compliant (verified in a headless render: every computed font-size lands on 12/14/16/20/28/36, only 12px/24px/50% radii, swatch ink picked by WCAG crossover rather than white-on-shadow); it previously had 7 off-scale sizes and 2 below the 12px floor. Re-audit: `design-audit/DRIFT-REPORT-2026-08-12.md` — Phase 1 held (weight-500 at **zero** occurrences site-wide, down from 135), but the type scale is *slipping*: 13px grew 353 → 401 and sub-12px 323 → 372, because the ruling is documented and not enforced by tooling. Also recorded: the Figma `Design System` page carries 16 components with no shared implementation in `src/components/ui/`, and there is no spacing/layout scale at all — Dashboard 1100 / Games 1024 / About 1200 / Talks 960 / brand 900. Prior update: 2026-08-12 (**A condition written as a comment is not a condition** (§26): the three Graduation Day modules shipped with their four intention follow-ups marked `"_note": "CONDITIONAL — only shown if Likert response is 2 or higher (not Never)"`, but `_note` is inert prose and `InterventionPage` navigation was strictly linear, so every participant was walked through "When will you practice? How often?" — *including* anyone who had just answered "Never". The intent was in the data from the start; only the mechanism was missing. Training modules now support **`show_if`**, a real conditional keyed to an earlier step's authored `key` (never its position), where an unmet condition saves no `intervention_responses` row at all, keeping "did not qualify" distinct from "left it empty". Norm's call was to make the gate an explicit yes/no question rather than a threshold on the slider — which also retires the open "should this scale start at 0 = Never?" question, since Nevers no longer reach the slider. Prior update: **Writing exam items against the Field Guide is a guide audit** (§29b): six holes found and catalogued as the first `kind='curated'` gaps — all six inside sections that already hold prose, which is exactly what `populate_page_gaps()` can never derive. Prior update: **Sandy Study 3 pilot fixes two defects in the manipulation itself** (§22, §24a). The N=20 Prolific pilot showed Word Probe's percentile curve needed 15 points for the 50th percentile, so **14/20 participants scored exactly 0** while 11 of those 14 were actively guessing — effort punished with no signal — which dragged the ``avg_pct`` every score display depends on down to a mean of 39 for people told to aim for the top 10%. Word Probe now awards partial credit per valid guess with a doubled solve bonus (strictly monotone: solve-on-1 = 13 … solve-on-6 = 8, fail = 6) on a recalibrated curve; replaying the pilot log gives stuck-at-zero 14/20 → 3/20 and ``avg_pct`` 39.2 → 50.4. Separately, the redemption arm's "new overall score" was the arithmetic **sum** of two percentiles, exceeding 100 for 13/20 (max 170) — now the mean, floored at the Aptitude percentile so a redemption can never lower a participant's standing. Both verified by replay against the real pilot data before shipping. Prior update: **Workbench capture is now per-session opt-in** (§29c) — Norm caught the design before it reached his machine. The original shipped "capture everything in a hooked repo, let sharing control who sees it", and his question (*"I don't want every session to start backing up, just when I ask"*) exposed that this is continuous background recording of all his work in the repo: **"nobody can see it yet" is not the same promise as "it was never recorded"**, and only the second is worth making about someone's own working notes. `workbench.json` now says only *where* and *how* to push; `scripts/workbench-share.mjs on <session-id>` says *whether*, one session at a time, publishing from the session's start. Accepted cost: an un-opted-in session is gone and cannot be shared retroactively. Endpoint verified live end to end — authenticated GET, POST write, and the scrubber turning a planted `sk-ant-…` into `[anthropic-key-redacted]` in the production row. Two env-var traps found on the way: the service key must be a new-scheme `sb_secret_…`, not the legacy `service_role` JWT (the endpoint now says so itself), and the project allowlist matched paths by equality, silently declining every worktree session. Prior update: 2026-08-11 (**The Workbench** (§29c): lab members can now watch the Claude Code sessions Norm shares with them, live, at `/workbench`. Three decisions carry it. **Tool output is never collected** — what travels is prompts, prose, and a one-line headline per tool call, which is safe by construction rather than by scrubbing, and matters because sessions here routinely hold participant rows and shared-drive paths. **`role = 'lab'` is not the gate**: it already grants `/admin/*` and every student in the lab holds it, so gating on it would have shown every captured session to all of them while looking like access control — the share tables are the entire access story and the console is super-admin-only. **Capture is unconditional; sharing controls visibility**, so a session is shareable without Norm having predicted the interest before the work happened. Two departures from the handoff brief: no `lab_members` table (lab members already exist as `profiles.role = 'lab'`; a parallel roster would be a second source of truth) and append-only turn rows instead of a content blob (live updates become cheap inserts, re-pushes idempotent, history free). One bug caught before anything was wired up: merging consecutive assistant messages collapsed a real 4-hour session into **two turns**, the second of which would have grown forever without ever re-publishing — one turn per *message* is the only append-only unit, and the frontend regroups. Visibility proved live under `SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated`: with the session shared to one lab member, a second lab member saw **0 sessions and 0 turns**, and a member cannot read the share table to learn who else holds it. Outstanding: `SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY` + `WORKBENCH_PUSH_TOKEN` in Vercel, and no real push has travelled end to end yet. Prior update: 2026-08-06 (**Field Guide precheck recovered from the live DB with two dead regexes fixed, and the WP6 review/contribution plan set (run plan §38)** — the precheck objects had run for a day with no migration file; transcribing them back out of Postgres exposed that the word count split on `'\\s+'`, an escaped literal backslash that matches nothing, so **every student submission would have been blocked as *1 words*** — and that five of the ten `clinical_instruction` patterns used `\b` as a word boundary when **in Postgres ARE `\b` is the backspace character** (the boundary is `\y`), so "start with 20 mg daily" passed the rule written to stop it. Both survived the original fixture test, which is the transferable lesson: **assert on the value inside a finding, not on the finding's presence** — the good fixture's `too_short` was recorded as "59 words against a 60-word floor" when the count was actually 1. Prior update: 2026-08-06 (**The Field Guide gets a student contribution pipeline: `page_gaps`, an automated submission precheck, and a staff review page at `/academic/fieldguide/submissions`.** **The design decision is that the unit is the *ask*, not the annotation** — 301 `Needs research` markers average **2.39 distinct asks each**, so one row per marker gives a pool of 301, under half of what 200 students × 3 contributions needs; split on asks it is **675**, plus 62 empty sections = **737 gaps**, and that is what makes the cohort size feasible. Gaps key on `(page_id, ask_hash)` so a claim survives when neighbouring prose is edited, and `populate_page_gaps()` never deletes — vanished asks surface in `stale_gaps` rather than orphaning claims. **Difficulty is auto-seeded and explicitly a triage aid, not a classification**: the regex produced false positives in both directions (“the opioid crisis” matched the crisis-line rule, `\yAct\y` matched **Acceptance and Commitment Therapy**), and a `gap_review_queue` view now surfaces only the boundary cases — a **17-row** audit rather than a 737-row one. **The precheck exists because the arithmetic is brutal**: at 600 submissions the irreducible human step (opening the source and confirming it says what the student claims) is **50–100 hours a term**, so nine mechanical checks strip the rest first — the sharpest being `clinical_instruction`, which catches the likeliest novice failure of answering a lookup question and padding it with treatment advice. **Verified against deliberate fixtures**, and the duplicate-source check immediately caught a real duplicate. **Review links land on the section, not the page** — 666 of 737 gaps resolve to an anchor. Prior update: **Added a hidden /brand press-kit page** -- collects existing logo/crest assets (public/RADlab_Logo.svg, RADlab_Logo_light.svg, UofT_Logo.svg, the orphaned HQlogo*.png marks), the section 9 color tokens, and the three @fontsource families behind an unlinked route (src/pages/BrandAssets.jsx); no new assets, no schema change.) Prior update: 2026-08-03 (**Triaging the Field Guide backlog for student contribution produced a rule that is not about difficulty: what happens if this is answered wrongly and nobody catches it?** Green (student-owned) = a wrong answer is visibly wrong or harmless; amber (student-drafted, staff-verified) = a wrong answer is plausible-looking; **red (never student work) = a wrong answer reads as clinical instruction or creates compliance exposure**. Difficulty and risk come apart — several red items are *easy*, and that is the point: a confident benzodiazepine tapering schedule in a wiki other students read **is** clinical guidance whatever disclaimer sits above it. **The red set is 11 items across 10 pages**, and two of the highest-risk are now closed from **Canadian** guidelines. `sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic` (College of Family Physicians deprescribing guideline) carries the finding that a **strong** recommendation can rest on **low-quality** evidence when the strength derives from harms of continued use rather than from deprescribing trials — recommendation strength is not a restatement of evidence quality — plus the fact that **no trials compare tapering schedules to each other**. `opioid-use-disorder` (CRISM/CMAJ) gets **buprenorphine–naloxone as first-line** and the counter-intuitive **strong recommendation against withdrawal management alone**, which raises relapse and overdose death because tolerance falls faster than supply. **New house convention: red-set material is written in reporting register** — *the guideline says X*, not *do X* — with an explicit not-clinical-instruction note and a statement of the guideline’s own scope, since the commonest way to mislead is applying a guideline to a population it excludes. Prior update: **Body-diagram figure: five-stage silhouette artwork** — the `body_diagram` intervention block (InterventionPage, Liliana's study check-ins) previously drew a broken stickman (floating head, identical dots). Now it crossfades through five silhouette images (`public/assets/bodymap/stage1-5.png`, cropped from Norm's `resources/5sillhouettesV2.png`, each window centred on its figure's dark-pixel midpoint so the crossfade doesn't shift): baseline → gut glow (body) → +heart (feelings) → +brain (thoughts) → full aura (behaviour), advancing as the four sequential fields complete, with a pulsing amber dot marking the active field's region (gut/heart/brain). New unauthenticated dev harness at `/dev/body-diagram-preview` renders the real block in demoMode; verified there (stage crossfade via inline opacity, dot progression, Next gating). Prior update: **The Field Guide catalogue is complete — 131 of 131 pages written, and every wikilink in the corpus resolves.** The sleep bundle (six sources, four pages) closed `sleep-wake-disorders`’ last gap, wrote `circadian-rhythm-sleep-wake-disorders` and `hypersomnolence-disorder`, and took `brief-psychotic-disorder` because it was the only thing left. **Red links 1 → 0 — the first zero since the signal was introduced in WP2** (244 of 244 distinct link targets resolve). **The finding of the sweep: a remission rate is a property of the study’s horizon, not of the disorder.** Two sources on brief psychotic disorder looked contradictory — three of four adolescents fully remitted in one; 54% developed a persistent psychotic disorder in the other — until the transition curve reconciles them (10% at 3 months, 19% at 12, 30% at 24, 54% at 60), and the first study’s mean follow-up was 22.8 months. **Second finding: sleep medicine does not use the DSM.** A contemporary review of the circadian disorders defines all six subtypes by **ICSD-3** and never mentions DSM-5; ICD-11 files sleep-wake outside the mental disorders in Chapter 07; and the AASM hypersomnolence guideline makes **no recommendation at all for psychiatric hypersomnia** — so the sleepiness most likely to reach a psychology clinic falls between two specialties. That closed the overview’s `contested` gap with an observation about practice rather than an argument. **Content is no longer the binding constraint**: eight gaps remain across seven existing pages, after which the work is the review pass and publishing. Prior update: **The Lecture 8 block: `substance-intoxication` closes and seven catalogue pages get written — 13 sources, 8 pages.** Unwritten catalogue pages **10 → 3**, major-tier gaps **13 across 9 → 9 across 8**. **The finding that generalises is that what a source counts is not what the page is about**: a 1,344-case emergency-department series of "acute intoxication" turns out to be **55.7% intentional self-poisoning**, with psychiatric medications, NSAIDs and paracetamol outweighing recreational drugs and alcohol — so the sex ratio inverts depending on which intoxication is meant; a search for **pyromania** returns essentially nothing, and the 1.0% lifetime figure is for **fire-setting**, a behaviour measured with a single item, with **OR 12.38 for antisocial personality disorder**; and "misuse" of benzodiazepines moved **14.1% → 21.8%** when a survey rewrote its definition. **§19.6’s state-the-evidence-base-first rule earned its keep three times**, most sharply on the Brazilian Psychiatric Association acute-intoxication consensus, which **could not grade its own evidence by Oxford, GRADE or AMSTAR** and fell back on a Delphi where **only 52 of 102 proposed items cleared a 65% threshold**. `tobacco-use-disorder` is the deliberate contrast case — 136 trials, 64,640 participants, RR 1.55, GRADE high. **And a measurement flaw surfaced in the tracking itself**: `reference_worklist.annotation_count` only counts annotations on pages that still have a derived gap, so every annotation number previously reported was a filtered subset — the view says **33**, the corpus actually holds **298 across 139 pages**. Prior update: **The Field Guide gains `alternatives-to-categorical-diagnosis`, and the section argues that there is no such thing as "the dimensional alternative".** The gap was chosen over larger ones because it had **23 inbound wikilinks** — second only to `evidence-based-practice` — and the contested sections written across three earlier sweeps had been pointing readers at an argument that was not on the page. Four sources, one per item the old Needs-research marker named: **Krueger & Hobbs (2020)** on the DSM-5 Section III Alternative Model, **Conway et al. (2019)** on HiTOP, **Cuthbert (2014)** on RDoC, **Borsboom (2017)** on network theory. **The organising finding is that the four disagree with each other, not just with the DSM**: categories, the AMPD’s traits, HiTOP’s spectra and RDoC’s circuits all keep the common-cause model and argue about its shape, while network theory removes it — so HiTOP and network models, routinely taught as allies, rest on incompatible premises, and Conway et al. concede only that they are "not necessarily mutually exclusive". **And every one of the four is candid that it cannot yet do the DSM’s job**, so the categorical model is less defended by the evidence than left standing by the absence of a deployable replacement. Two side effects: the HiTOP source supplied the DSM-5 field-trial agreement figure (**~40% of diagnoses below the acceptable inter-rater cutoff**) that a *prose* sentence had been asking for since Module 3 — a declared debt no derived gap could see — and the AMPD source closed the matching annotation on `personality-disorders`. **Major-tier gaps are now 13 across 9 pages**, which makes publishing, not writing, the next binding constraint. Prior update: **Field Guide signup was emailing everyone a link to `localhost`.** Reported from a real attempt; two causes, one in code and one in configuration. **Code:** `FieldGuideAuthRoute` called `signUp()` with **no `emailRedirectTo`** — unlike `Signup.jsx` and `ForgotPassword.jsx`, which both pass `window.location.origin` — and with no `redirectTo` Supabase falls back to the project’s **Site URL**, which on radlab-academic is still a development URL. Signup now redirects to `/academic/fieldguide/wiki`, which sits under the guard, so the guard creates the course client, the client consumes the token in the URL, and its `onAuthStateChange` subscription re-renders signed in. **A second hazard turned up while fixing it, which would have broken the link even after redirecting correctly**: the Field Guide authenticates against a **different Supabase project**, but `src/lib/supabase.js` creates the main-site client with `detectSessionInUrl` on by default — so a confirmation link landing under `/academic/…` carries a token the main project cannot use, and the main client would have tried to consume it anyway, either writing another project’s session into this one’s storage or eating a single-use code before the academic client could exchange it. Detection is now disabled **only** on `/academic` paths; the main site’s own `/verified` and `/reset-password` flows still depend on it. **The configuration half is not in this repo**: Supabase ignores `emailRedirectTo` unless the URL is on the project’s **Redirect URLs** allow-list — their own troubleshooting page says exactly this — so **radlab-academic** needs Site URL **`https://radlab.zone`** and **`https://radlab.zone/**`** allow-listed. **Until that is set the code fix alone will not work.** Prior update: **The wiki index gets a card view, and the chapter icons become the browse rather than decoration on a heading.** Default is now a **grid of chapter cards with 96px icons**, title and coverage count — twenty diagnostic classes as one screen instead of twenty stacked headings. A **Cards / List** segmented control switches modes, and **Collapse all / Expand all appear in list view only**, because folding means nothing until the pages are on screen. **The bridge between the two views is the card click**: opening a chapter **switches to list, folds every other chapter, and scrolls to the one asked for** — opening in place, or landing in list with all twenty expanded, would lose the thing the click was for. Two details from mocking it against the real artwork first: **counts are pushed to the card bottom with `margin-top:auto`** so they line up across a row whose titles wrap to different numbers of lines, and **Foundations shows no number badge** rather than a placeholder dash, since it carries no DSM chapter. Prior update: **The *Smith v Jones* gap closes — Norm supplied the judgment, so it is written from the case rather than from memory.** CanLII 403s automated fetches; the PDF in `PSY240resources/` resolved it. **The permission-versus-duty distinction is now anchored in the procedural history rather than asserted**: the **trial judge held the psychiatrist was under a *duty* to disclose**, the **Court of Appeal varied that to an order *permitting* disclosure**, and the **Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the Court of Appeal**. The Canadian rule is what a clinician **may** do; *Tarasoff* is what a Californian clinician **must** do — and that changes where liability and discretion sit. **A second difference the page now makes explicit:** *Smith v Jones* is decided as a **solicitor-client privilege** case, the psychiatrist having been retained by defence counsel, where *Tarasoff* arose from a **therapeutic** relationship and a negligence claim — the doctrines have different parents. The **three factors** are on the page with the Court’s own qualifications: **clarity** (the person or group must be *ascertainable*; a general threat to a whole city may be too vague, though a large group can count if clearly identified), **seriousness**, and **imminence** — which must create *a sense of urgency* but **may apply to some time in the future**, with no particular time limit required. They are **weighted, not counted**, and if the test is met **disclosure is still limited to the information necessary to protect public safety**. **The dissent is on the page too**, because it makes the clinical argument the majority does not: the breach must be **as narrow as possible**, and the psychiatrist should disclose his opinion and that it rests on a consultation but **not the accused’s own account of the offence**, which risks becoming **conscriptive evidence**. Their reasoning is itself a public-safety argument — a narrow exception **fosters a climate in which dangerous individuals disclose, seek treatment and pose less danger**, this accused having been diagnosed **only because he felt secure in confiding**. That is the strongest available statement of the cost side of any duty-to-warn rule, and it comes from inside the Court that created the Canadian exception. The divergence is **deliberate**: the Court **considered *Tarasoff*** directly, with *Thompson v. County of Alameda*, *Brady v. Hopper* and *W. v. Egdell*. Handled as a **primary legal source, not a licensed article** — public SCC judgment, paraphrase and short quotation, facts kept at **headnote level** (the category of threat and the identified victim group are load-bearing for the clarity factor; no method detail), recorded in `result_json.editorial_note`. `law-and-ethics` is now **25,225 characters, four sources, no declared gaps**. Prior update: **`law-and-ethics` gets its Canadian content — and the article that was asked for turns out not to exist.** The brief was a paper outlining how the Canadian mental health and justice system differs from the US. **There is no such paper in the biomedical literature**: searches across NCRMD, forensic psychiatry, civil commitment, duty to warn, insanity defence and health-system comparison returned nothing, because comparative mental-health *law* scholarship lives in law journals (CanLII, *Health Law Journal*) that PubMed and Europe PMC do not index. **One near-miss is the lesson**: *"Cross-Cultural Notions of Risk and Liberty: A Comparison of Involuntary Psychiatric Hospitalization…"* reads from its title like exactly the paper wanted and in fact compares **New York and Zurich**, with Canada nowhere in it — fetch before assuming from a title, on the search side as well as the citation side. The route taken instead was **Canadian primary sources**, which is arguably better: the page now states Canadian law directly and lets the US material already there provide the contrast. **Both declared gaps close.** From the **National Trajectory Project** (1,800 people found NCRMD across Quebec, Ontario and BC): **Criminal Code s.16**, the Review Board structure — federal provisions, **provincial administration**, minimum yearly review, three dispositions — and findings that run hard against the public image of the verdict. **Homicide and attempted murder are under 7% of all NCRMD verdicts**; the largest categories are **threats (27.4%)** and **assaults (26.5%)**; and **33.7% of victims were family or partners against 22.7% strangers**, rising to **60.8% family or partners** for homicide specifically. **70.9%** had a psychotic-spectrum diagnosis and **72%** a prior psychiatric hospitalisation — so this is mostly people already known to services who threatened or assaulted someone close to them, a different problem from the one the insanity defence is usually argued about. **Provincial variation is large and the authors decline to explain it**, and the records differ in completeness (education missing from 44.1% of Quebec files against 5.4% in BC) — **a national figure conceals three systems**. On the ethics side, the **Canadian Academy of Psychiatry and the Law** guidelines supply a role separation the page had not made: the forensic assessor is **not** the treating clinician and must be **independent of the retaining party**, and **consent inverts** — the requirement is to explain **the limits of confidentiality** before starting, because the person being assessed is often not the client. **And one thing could not be sourced and was not faked.** **CanLII 403s automated fetches**, so ***Smith v Jones* (1999 SCC) has no source** and was **not written from memory**; the page still declares it, now as the single most important correction it needs — disclosure as a public-safety **exception to privilege**, a *permission*, against the affirmative *duty* that *Tarasoff* imposed. The CAPL guidelines cannot close it either: they **explicitly decline duty to warn and cite no case law at all**, which the page records so the next session knows the obvious document is not the answer. Prior update: **The paraphilias close — the cluster with the weakest existing content, fixed with four open-access reviews.** Six pages across Lecture 7, including both Tier A pages and the chapter overview; major-tier gaps **21 → 16**, `treatment` **18 → 11**, `etiology` **15 → 11**. **The finding that reorganises the chapter is a null result**: a neuroimaging meta-analysis of **436 men with pedophilic disorder against 449 controls found no structural brain difference**. Since pedophilic disorder is by far the most-researched paraphilia, a null there is the strongest available statement about the whole chapter — and it means the three circulating neurobiological models (frontal-dysexecutive, temporal-limbic, dual-dysfunction) explain **hypersexuality and disinhibition** while **none explains the paraphilic interest itself**. **Acquired cases argue against the models they are cited to support**: 64 documented cases, 63 male, mean onset **52.8**, **81% with no premorbid interest**, arriving alongside hyperphagia, kleptomania, aggression and compulsivity — a general failure of behavioural filtering, sometimes with no corresponding sexual fantasies at all. A lesion that removes inhibition tells you about inhibition, so such cases **should not be used to infer the neurology of the developmental disorder**. **The treatment sections open with what the evidence does not show**, because the review does: testosterone-lowering drugs reduce sexual *activity*, and **risk of offending was not assessed in any of the randomised trials** — median sample **13.5**, median follow-up **15 weeks**, one study after 2010, and harms including **two cases of increased suicidal ideation** on degarelix and a European restriction on cyproterone over meningioma risk. **Adding psychotherapy has not been shown to add anything on this evidence** (drug alone vs desensitisation alone vs both: no significant differences), which is worth holding against the overview’s summary that combined treatment is superior. **The whole pharmacological base for the chapter is 28 studies and 379 people, only three of 28 scoring above 5 on Newcastle-Ottawa** — stated on every paraphilia page before any drug is named. Two asymmetries the sources ignore are now named on the pages: **sadism and masochism are two different treatment questions** (one a distress diagnosis, the other a harm-to-others one) and the drug literature was built for the second; and **fetishistic disorder is the one paraphilia where conditioning has been studied**, so a learning account predicts behavioural treatment is where the leverage is — recorded as a gap rather than filled with drug evidence answering a different question. The **WFSBP guideline usually cited here is adolescent-specific**; it was fetched, read and deliberately *not* used as general guidance, but it explains the shape of the field: **ethical constraints make placebo-controlled designs very difficult in potential offenders**. Prevention services are named as protective information — **Dunkelfeld**, **Stop It Now**, **Preventell**, **Don’t Offend India**. All four sources are used for etiology, treatment and prevention only; no offence detail appears, and the decision is recorded in `result_json.editorial_note`. Live: **252 pages**, 1,383 wikilinks, 146 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The Field Guide gets chapter icons, and the wiki index folds by chapter.** Norm supplied a 2048×2048 composite of 20 watercolour glyphs, one per DSM-5-TR diagnostic class. **The tiles were located by decoding the PNG and reading its ink profile rather than by eyeballing coordinates** — a first estimate drifted far enough by the bottom-right corner to slice the artwork in half, while column/row ink bands resolved the grid exactly: **310×318 boxes at x = 101/485/869/1253/1637 and y = 101/571/1063/1603**. Columns had to be measured *inside* each icon row, because label text is often wider than the box it sits under and inflates a whole-image profile. **The grid duplicates "Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders"** at positions 15 and 16 (identical artwork, so nothing is lost by skipping one), and has no tile for **ch.20 Other Mental Disorders**, which the course omits anyway — so **19 icons for chapters 1-19**, sliced with ffmpeg (Windows’ `convert` on PATH is the FAT converter, not ImageMagick) to 192px WebP at **~2.6 KB each, 50 KB for the set**. They render in the **index chapter headings** and the **article breadcrumb**; a chapter with no file renders **no icon rather than a broken image**, so a partial set degrades to the text-only layout. Files **register themselves** — `chapterIcons.js` globs `src/assets/chapter-icons/<chapter number>.<name>.webp`, so there is no manifest to drift. **One build detail worth keeping:** most of these sit under Vite’s 4 KB inline threshold, so by default 16 of 19 were **base64’d into a shared 56 KB chunk that every wiki page had to download to show one 22px icon**; `query: '?no-inline&url'` forces separate files, dropping that chunk to **5.5 KB of URLs** and making `loading="lazy"` mean something. Prior update: **The wiki reader gets collapsible sections.** Pages now run 8-20k characters, so every `##` section folds from its own heading, with **Collapse all / Expand all** and a live "*n* of *m* folded" count above the body. **The hard part was anchors, not the fold.** Section bodies are rendered as *slices* of the page, and `react-markdown` numbers lines from the start of whatever string it is handed — so a slice would silently give its headings the ids belonging to the top of the page, breaking every table-of-contents link and every inbound `[[page#section]]`. `splitSections()` therefore returns a **`startLine`** with each slice and `WikiMarkdown` takes it as a **`lineOffset`**, resolving anchors against ids computed once over the whole body; leading blank lines are stripped *and the offset moves with them*, which is the off-by-one that would otherwise put every anchor one line short. Section ids come from `extractHeadings()` rather than being re-slugified, because that function **de-duplicates repeated headings** (`presentation`, `presentation-2`) and real pages do repeat the six-section skeleton. Clicking a folded section in the contents, or arriving on a `#section` deep link, **opens the section that owns the anchor first and scrolls on the next frame** — including for a `###` nested inside a folded `##`, which is why each section carries the list of anchor ids it contains. Fold state is **stamped with its slug**, the same idiom the page row already uses, so navigating away starts unfolded and no effect is needed to reset it. **Everything starts expanded** — find-in-page cannot see unmounted text, so a reference wiki that opened folded would hide the thing it was opened for. Verified against a real page plus synthetic cases covering an H1 preamble, duplicate `##` and `###` headings, a `##` inside a fenced code block, a page with no `##` at all, and an empty body: **section ids match the contents, no content is lost, and every anchor resolves**. Prior update: **Alongside's aversive audio is replaced by two cellos (§29b)** — a 4.1 kHz tone gated by an 11 Hz square, a 0.5 Hz-beating drone that swelled as you travelled, and a noise-burst on every dissolve, all gone. The wisp and the traveller are each a faint bowed string on D3 and **distance is intonation**: sour fifth at the band edges, gliding true through the companion band (measured 0 cents together, −67 apart). Prior update: 2026-08-03 (**Lecture 10 goes clear, and the chapter map gets the chapter the catalogue had deliberately left out.** `communication-disorders` — the last multi-gap page in the lecture — closed **epidemiology, etiology, treatment and contested** from four CC BY sources, and now runs 19,215 chars with five sources and no declared gaps. **Ascertainment decides the answer twice on that one page**: heritability is **0.97 in clinically ascertained twins and near zero in population-screened twins**, and the long-standing male predominance **vanishes in an unselected birth cohort** (52.9% male, p = 0.799), which the authors attribute to referral bias toward boys and under-detection of girls — **a sex ratio from clinic samples measures who gets referred**. The same cohort found **only 2 of 104 children meeting criteria had ever been identified by a health professional**, which sits directly against the diagnostic review’s conclusion that there is **insufficient evidence for universal screening**; both are on the page. **The treatment evidence runs the wrong way relative to the epidemiology** — expressive targets have RCT support (SMD 0.44-1.08) while **receptive vocabulary has no studies at all**, and **46.2% of affected children have combined receptive-expressive difficulties** — and the one long follow-up found gains **gone by age 6 with controls caught up**, i.e. acceleration rather than a changed outcome. Underneath all of it, **the nosology limits the genetics**: studies use language cutoffs from **1.25 to 2.0 SD** with inconsistent IQ thresholds because no international diagnostic consensus exists, so samples cannot be pooled and results do not replicate. **And elimination disorders now has a page.** It existed nowhere — no page, no catalogue row — which was **not an oversight**: `dsm_chapters` records **Chapter 11 as `taught = false`**, one of two chapters so marked. But a Field Guide that silently omits a whole DSM chapter reads as incomplete rather than scoped, so it is written as an **explicitly out-of-scope overview**, catalogued with `tier = overview` and **`lecture = NULL`** (catalogue 130 → 131). Its justification is the part a psychology course would use: **20-30% of children with enuresis and 30-50% with encopresis have a clinically relevant comorbid disorder, over a fourfold increase on peers** — and where effects reach significance they are **externalising** (attention, social problems, self-concept, aggression) while **depression and anxiety do not differ significantly**, the null being the surprise. The rule both pages produced: **where a page covers less than its title claims, repeat the scope limit in the section carrying the numbers**, not only in a note at the top that gets read once. Live: **252 pages**, 1,361 wikilinks, 138 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The neurocognitive chapter closes — 13 pages, zero declared gaps, the first DSM chapter in the corpus to be finished.** Four more sources completed it (Outeiro 2019 for Lewy body pathogenesis and Parkinson’s disease dementia, Jurcau 2024 for prion disease, Anderson 2018 for Huntington’s, Vastag 2022 for HIV), including the last unwritten catalogue page. **Two structural findings.** First, **a composite page can define its own section scheme**: `neurocognitive-disorder-other-aetiologies` is one slug covering four unrelated diseases, so it uses `##` headings *per disease* instead of the standard six — and the gap machinery works **better** that way, because `extract_page_sections()` keys on any `##` heading, so each unwritten aetiology surfaced as its own named gap (`huntingtons-disease`, `parkinsons-disease-dementia`…) and closed independently. **The standard six are a default for single-disorder pages, not a schema.** Second, **a four-source page needs four sequential versions** — provenance joins version to job, so the page was created with three diseases as explicit placeholders and each later version replaced exactly one, leaving every intermediate state honest about what it was missing and the finished page carrying **4 sources** under *Built from*. **The finding the chapter kept producing, now visible because the pages are adjacent: removing the pathological protein has failed to help in three separate diseases.** The **PRN100** antibody **cleared PrP-scrapie with no effect on clinical progression**; lecanemab and donanemab clear amyloid for differences **below the threshold of perception**; and **Lewy body density does not correlate with duration, onset, fluctuations, hallucinations, delusions, falls, parkinsonism or cognitive decline** — with *in vitro* work suggesting **fibril uptake is protective while monomer and oligomer uptake triggers apoptosis**, which would make the structure the disease is named after the brain’s defence. **And knowing the cause turns out to buy less than expected**: Huntington’s has a single testable autosomal dominant mutation and management resting on **expert consensus** for want of trial data; prion disease is understood in molecular detail and **every therapeutic attempt has failed**. Also on the record: **DLB and Parkinson’s disease dementia are separated by a one-year rule its own authors call arbitrary**, with end-stage neuropathology that may be identical; the **Frascati criteria** for HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder produce **false positives in 15-22% of people without HIV**; the Huntington guidance says to **cut the SSRI or neuroleptic before treating apathy**, because drug-induced apathy is indistinguishable from the disease; and in rapidly progressive dementia **the expensive error is missing the reversible mimic** — thiamine deficiency can produce the same cortical ribboning on MRI as CJD. Live: **251 pages**, 1,353 wikilinks, 132 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The Lecture 10 neurocognitive sweep — and the discovery that a page can be complete and still be wrong.** Nine sources, eight pages, two of them new; `treatment` gaps **23 → 18**. The finding that changes the review method: **`neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-alzheimers-disease` had a full treatment section, no declared gap, and a sentence calling disease-modifying therapy "research in its infancy"** — accurate to its source, the Alzheimer’s Association **2017**, and false by 2026, because **lecanemab and donanemab had completed phase 3 and appeared nowhere on the page**. The gap query cannot find this class of error: `needs` only surfaces what a page *declares* missing, and a confidently-written stale section declares nothing. **New standing check: for every page, what is the newest source, and has the field moved since** — with treatment sections and advocacy-organisation citations the most exposed, since presentation ages slowly and treatment does not. The replacement is the corpus’s best worked example of **relative-versus-absolute framing**: lecanemab’s "27% slowing" is **0.45 points on an 18-point scale (2.5%)** and donanemab’s "33%" is **3.4 on a 144-point scale (2.4%)** — **both below the minimal clinically important difference on both scales** — against 45% and 89% treatment-related adverse events, brain swelling or bleeding in a quarter to a third, and a **number needed to harm of about three**. **Both sources are partisan, in opposite directions** (Espay/Kepp/Herrup are prominent critics; **Selkoe originated the amyloid cascade hypothesis**), which turned out to be an advantage: the page names both positions and then mines **what both sides concede** — that the field **has no validated definition of clinical meaningfulness**, that the aducanumab approval was reconciled by a **post-hoc** reanalysis its own defenders call post-hoc, and that the trials **may not measure the toxic species**, since soluble oligomers are invisible to amyloid PET. Elsewhere in the chapter: **delirium prevention works and delirium treatment does not** (multicomponent programmes cut incidence, **RR 0.71** after hip fracture, but *"the available evidence does not support the efficacy"* of the same interventions once delirium has started — and no benefit at all in low-risk patients); **donepezil helps after TBI, is recommended for deprescribing in mild neurocognitive disorder, and worsened disinhibition in 4 of 12 patients with frontotemporal dementia**, which is the argument for subtyping stated in the only currency that matters; **two dementias where the standard response to agitation is the dangerous one** (fatal antipsychotic sensitivity in Lewy body disease, parkinsonism and tardive antecollis in bvFTD); and **oral thiamine is not a weaker treatment for Wernicke encephalopathy but not a treatment at all**, while requiring the classic triad finds **23%** of cases against **85%** for Caine’s two-of-four criteria. Two new pages: **`neurocognitive-disorder-with-lewy-bodies`** and **`substance-medication-induced-neurocognitive-disorder`**, the latter carrying the chapter’s only good news — alcohol-related impairment **partially reverses** over a year or more of abstinence, with increased brain volume. Live: **250 pages**, 1,343 wikilinks, 127 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **Reply gains a register economy (§29b)** — six creature personas each fix a home pitch, a constellation motion and an idle chirp cadence at once; a voice answers by transposing your phrase's contour into its own register, and trusted voices chirp on their own, so **the night fills in proportion to how much of the pitch ladder you have courted** (measured: ~10 chirps/90s from 2 low types when only the low end is courted, ~19 from 4 spread types across the full ladder). Prior update: 2026-08-03 (**Five Come, See dynamics prototypes ship as a static sketchbook at `/prototypes/` (§29b)** — Thaw, Milkweed, Reply, Alongside, Stone: the five never-built receptive dynamics from the Come, See design compendium (§4 of that doc), each a self-contained 3–5-minute canvas testbed with diegetic-only feedback and a `window.__<name>` debug API. Every one was adversarially playtested by an agent that *played* it headlessly and measured the physics; the fix passes closed real principle violations — dead fog-regrowth from canvas 1/255 alpha quantization, a valley bricked for 252 s by 20 s of tapping, content exhaustion at 2.5 min, a companion teleporting out of view, a night that was a waiting room — plus a five-page visual QA sweep. No app-bundle impact: inert static files under `public/prototypes/`.) Prior update: 2026-08-03 (**Prevalence becomes an invariant, a concept page and a reader surface.** All **108 disorder pages** now carry a one-line `prevalence:` value in frontmatter — previously 63 had one, 12 held a placeholder and **33 had no such field at all**, and *none* of the three states was visible, because the reader never rendered the field. **21 of the 108 honestly report that no rate exists**, written out rather than left blank, because blank means nobody looked while **"largely unknown — deception is intrinsic to the disorder and clinicians rarely record the diagnosis"** means somebody looked and the absence has a reason; on `pedophilic-disorder` stigma makes clinical samples unrepresentative *by construction*, and `voyeuristic-disorder` records that the source’s own two figures contradict each other **in the same passage** and must not be quoted. **Values are derived from each page’s own already-provenanced Epidemiology section**, so no new claim enters the corpus and the frontmatter cannot drift from the body — which is why it ran as a plain `UPDATE` rather than an ingest, with the five `wiki_pages` triggers doing the snapshot/needs/links/touch bookkeeping and **link count unchanged at 1,286** across the 45-page edit as the check that no bodies moved. **New `prevalence` concept page**, deliberately not a duplicate of `epidemiology` (which keeps the definitions): it carries what the contested campaign kept turning up — that a rate is a property of **the manual, the instrument, the threshold and the sample**, demonstrated by delirium (**the same 200 patients are 16% or 28% delirious depending which book is open**), agoraphobia (**prevalence unchanged between DSM-IV and DSM-5 while 43% of cases are recognised by one manual and not the other**) and health anxiety (**41 different measures, most without a validated cut-off, giving 4.3%-86% across 58 cancer studies — and 28%-70% even holding the instrument and cut-off constant**). Built as **three sequential versions under three jobs** so all three sources appear under *Built from*. **And the label is the link**: `WikiPage.jsx` now renders the value under the summary with "Prevalence" linking to the concept page, which gives **all 108 disorder pages a route there without editing 108 bodies** — the alternative would have added ~108 graph edges of no analytical value, so the page keeps **one** real backlink and the graph stays meaningful. Live: **248 pages**, 1,300 wikilinks, 117 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The `contested` campaign completes Tier A: 24 pages closed from 20 open-access journal sources, `contested` empty 47 → 21, and every centrally-important page in the corpus now has a critique section.** The method that made it affordable is the transferable part: **batch the Europe PMC REST API over a topic list**, print `pmcid | year | journal | title` for 15-20 topics in one shell loop, shortlist, and only then fetch — with the **verification fetch still mandatory before writing**, because a search hit gives a title, not a citation and not a licence. **World Psychiatry alone does not cover the course**: 17 topics returned nothing for phobia, dissociation, delirium, Alzheimer’s, narcolepsy, adjustment disorder, PMDD, schizoaffective or delusional disorder; widening to BMC Psychiatry, Frontiers in Psychiatry, PLOS ONE, F1000Research, Dialogues in Clinical Neuroscience, Depression and Anxiety, Nature and Science of Sleep and World Journal of Psychiatry closed almost all of them — **search the topic, not the journal**. **The recurring teaching finding is that prevalence is a property of the manual**: the same **200 delirium patients** yield **28% under DSM-III-R, 27% DSM-5, 21% DSM-IV, 16% ICD-10**, and ICD-10 **misses 47% of cases**; agoraphobia’s prevalence is unchanged between DSM-IV and DSM-5 while **43% of cases are recognised by one manual and not the other**. **Reliability and accuracy trade off against each other** — DSM-5’s delirium criteria are the most reliable of four systems and slightly less accurate, and *disorganised thinking* was dropped after DSM-III-R **to help non-psychiatrists agree** despite performing well; DSM-5 collapsed primary and secondary insomnia because **the mechanism is poorly understood**, not because the distinction failed. **Thresholds that decide who gets treated are often arbitrary**: the Y-BOCS **16** used as trial-entry criterion across the OCD literature has **no empirical basis**, and the empirically derived “severe” cut of 30 has PPV 43-49%, leading its own authors to say rationing specialist care by it **should be questioned**. Three pages needed their **denominator stated before their findings** — `adjustment-disorders` (a qualitative study of **four people**), `dissociative-amnesia` (**22 studies, 49 patients, mean quality 4.9/10**), `specific-phobia` (**3 of 33 studies used clinical samples**, in a population defined by not seeking treatment). And **sources that are parties to their own dispute are now a pattern, not an exception** — Brand et al. on DID and the ESSM statement on erectile dysfunction join Volkow on addiction: name the authorship position in the page text, then use the source’s own numbers. **Licences varied per article, not per journal** — a WHO-authored piece in a copyrighted journal is CC BY; four sources are CC BY-NC-ND and are cite-and-paraphrase only. Live: **247 pages**, 1,286 wikilinks, 11 red links all to real catalogue slugs, 114 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The `contested` campaign opens, and the gap analysis changed the plan.** Querying what the corpus still declares missing showed **`contested` is now the largest hole — 47 pages, 38% of all empty sections**, 22 of them Tier A, ahead of `treatment` (27), `etiology` (19) and `epidemiology` (11). **More textbooks will not close it**: five in, every one supplied presentation/prevalence/etiology/treatment and every one left `contested` empty on most pages, because critique is a different genre. So the source strategy shifts from textbooks to **open-access journals**, using the vehicle the corpus already has — the `debate` page type and the journal-article ingest. **Proof of concept: PTSD**, from **Bryant (2019), *World Psychiatry* 18(3):259-269**, verified on PMC before use. It produced the best `contested` section in the corpus: **only 42% of trauma survivors are diagnosed under *both* DSM-5 and ICD-11** — two manuals, the same people, agreement on fewer than half the cases, which reframes every prevalence figure on the page including the Canadian ones; **636,120 permutations** of how DSM-5 PTSD may present, which is Bryant’s explanation for why biomarkers have not been found; a real cost on both sides of the breadth/specificity trade-off, since **moving beyond fear symptoms undermines the evidence base of the exposure treatments the page recommends**; complex PTSD surviving its validity test against borderline personality disorder; and **only two-thirds responding adequately to trauma-focused CBT**, which Bryant reads as a failure of the *category* presenting as a failure of treatment. **Licence handled conservatively** — the PMC record shows © World Psychiatric Association with no explicit CC statement in the retrieved metadata, so cite-and-paraphrase only, the same treatment as StatPearls and the NAP gambling source, recorded in `licence_note`. **And the campaign is per-page, not per-source**, which is the planning point: each target needs a search, a **verification fetch**, a read and a write, and searches for OCD, bipolar, panic and GAD returned mostly non-World-Psychiatry work, so coverage cannot be assumed. **Never write a citation from a search-result summary** — one candidate that looked like Brewin’s 2025 PTSD review turned out to be **Maercker’s commentary on it**, and the Wiley copy 403s to automated fetch; both caught by fetching before writing. A fabricated citation in a reference corpus is worse than an empty section. Live: **245 pages**, 1,186 wikilinks, 0 off-catalogue red links, 85 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The Field Guide gets its first student-facing page, and the corpus’s highest-priority safety gap closes.** `student-support-resources`, from Kulzhabayeva (2026), *Mental Health and Student Support Resources* — internal RADlab material compiled 2026-07-20, used with the lab’s own authority for its own course. It replaces the **US-only 988 line** that was all `suicide-and-self-harm` could offer: now the **9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline** (call or text 988, free and confidential anywhere in Canada, 24h), **Good2Talk** for Ontario post-secondary students, **U of T TELUS Health Student Support** (24h, all students), all three campus health centres with same-day routing for St. George, and **Find-A-Helpline** for students outside Canada. Worth knowing for anyone reading the literature: **Canada and the US share the 988 digits**, so a paper citing "988" may mean either service, and the pages say so. **Two editorial decisions.** The source ends with a study-specific research contact — it was written to appear at the end of a *different* study’s surveys — and that was **omitted deliberately**, since directing PSY240 students to another study’s investigator would misdirect them; the omission is recorded in the job so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight. And the page **states why it exists from the course’s own findings**: ~60% of people with suicidal thoughts do not seek help, citing **low perceived need and wanting to handle it alone** rather than unavailable treatment, while only ~10% of people with gambling disorder ever seek treatment — **the barrier the literature identifies is knowledge and reluctance, not scarcity**, which is exactly what a visible, specific list addresses. That makes the page an application of the content rather than boilerplate appended to it. **It also introduces a standing obligation the corpus did not previously have.** This is the one page where a stale detail could cause direct harm, so it carries a visible warning, a `staleness_warning` on the job, and a `verify_before_publishing: true` frontmatter flag so a publication pass can find it **by query rather than by memory**: re-verify every entry before students get access and at the start of each term, and **remove any number that cannot be verified rather than publish it unchecked**. Open question left to Norm: it has **one inbound link**, so it sits one hop from most sensitive material — which is a real barrier for a reader in distress, but where to place trigger-adjacent signposting across a course is a pedagogical call, and run plan §17.4 sets out the bounded rule if wanted. Live: **245 pages**, 1,172 wikilinks, 0 off-catalogue red links, 84 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **The sweep completes — every section of all five sources is in.** The remaining Cummings sections and Davies chapters produced **one new page and nine gap-closing updates**, and the ordering principle is the transferable part: **gap-first, not source-first.** The declared `needs`/`annotations` lists were queried first and only the sections that could close them were read — **nine of ten items closed a specific declared gap**, and all ten pages now have **zero empty sections**, with corpus empty sections falling **129 → 123** despite four new pages in the same period. Sweeping section by section produces bulk; sweeping against a gap list produces closure. **The MTA trial closed the longest-standing declared gap in the corpus**, and its result is better than either side of the medication debate reports: stimulant medication was most effective on core symptoms and combined treatment was no better — but behavioural treatment produced **less school disruption, lower required stimulant doses and higher parent satisfaction**, so a single headline result is not a treatment recommendation. **The ADHD parenting myth is refuted by an unusually clean design**: Cunningham and Barkley found mothers of children with ADHD less attentive and more controlling, then showed that **giving the children stimulants improved the mothers’ parenting to the level of mothers of typically developing children** — the arrow runs child → parent, and a brief interaction with an impulsive child even raised parents’ alcohol consumption. **Moral treatment and deinstitutionalisation failed the same way a century apart** — moral treatment worked best at ≤200 patients, immigration pushed facilities past 1,000, funding collapsed, and **immigrants were denied the treatment given to native-born citizens even where resources existed** — so the recurring failure is **resourcing and equity, not the humane principle**. The institutional model **arrived in Canada as imperial policy** (County Asylums Act 1845 extended to the colonies after a Kingston, Jamaica audit), which *partially* closes the non-Western histories gap and the page says so. **Szasz is now on the record properly**, including the argument’s decisive vindication — he was perhaps the first psychiatrist to challenge homosexuality as a diagnosis — held against `gender-dysphoria`, where the same argument is live and removing the diagnosis would also remove funded care: **the critique was right once, which does not make it automatically right again.** New **`psychopharmacology`** page supplies what the medication pages lacked: ADME, route of administration predicting abuse liability, the grapefruit-juice interaction (85 drugs), the **four metaboliser categories where both extremes look like treatment failure and neither is**, and the two populations excluded from the trials that licensed their drugs. **Two sections were read and produced nothing** — Cummings 5.1 and 7.1 have no substantive Canadian prose; an earlier keyword count suggested otherwise because it was matching **reference-list entries**. **Count hits in the body, not the references** — a citation to a Canadian journal is not Canadian content, and the earlier §11 scan overstated coverage on that basis. And the pre-accept checks caught **two more structural errors** before acceptance — duplicated headings and a block landing in the wrong section — the third consecutive run in which they caught something real. Prior update: **The skeleton is complete: Tier A 54/54, foundations 14/14, overviews 16/16.** `suicide-and-self-harm` was the last page and had been the most-linked red link in the corpus at **11 inbound references** — eleven disorder pages each reporting suicide risk with nowhere to point. Source: **Davies (2025) ch 22**, adapted from Coursehero under CC BY-SA. **Safe messaging was applied and cost the page nothing analytically**: the source carries a named-individual case study with circumstantial detail, and the page omits circumstances and method entirely while keeping the teaching point — that risk is often invisible to those closest to the person, so **absence of visible warning signs is not evidence of absence of risk**. Means-restriction evidence is retained, because that is protective public-health content rather than method information; the distinction is the one to apply next time, and an `editorial_note` on the job records the decision so it is not silently reversed. **The organising finding is the ideation gap**: roughly **10.6 million US adults with serious suicidal thoughts** against **1.4 million attempts** and **47,000 deaths**, with prevention research, clinical treatment and health policy all organised around the two smaller numbers (Jobes & Joiner, 2019) — a field that measures what it can count under-serves the largest affected group. **The treatment evidence is the strongest in the corpus and unusually comes with magnitudes**: Crisis Response Plan **−76% attempts** at 6 months against no-harm contracts; Brief CBT **−60%** at 24 months; CT-SP **−50%** at 18 months; CAMS as good as DBT on attempts; and Motto & Bostrom’s **caring letters** — a note every four months for five years — reducing suicides. The pattern is the teachable part: **treatments targeting suicidality *directly* outperform treating an underlying disorder and expecting risk to follow**, which runs against how the rest of the course handles comorbidity. Coercive **no-harm contracts** have been displaced by **stabilization planning** — a clean case of a standard practice retired on evidence. The limiting barrier is that **~60% of people with suicidal thoughts do not seek help**, citing low perceived need and wanting to handle it alone rather than unavailable treatment. **Two gaps are flagged on the page, one urgent**: non-suicidal self-injury is in the title and absent from the source; and the crisis line is **US-only (988)**, so the **Canadian 9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline and provincial services must be added with the number and hours verified before publishing** — the single highest-priority verification item in the corpus, since it is the one line a student in distress might act on. **Only Tier B is now incomplete, at 33/46.** Live: **243 pages**, 1,149 wikilinks, 15 red links all resolving to real catalogue slugs, 0 blue links to an empty page, 74 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Prior update: **Tier A is complete at 54/54.** `gambling-disorder` — the last uncovered Tier A page, and the one no textbook in the corpus touched — written from two sources with **materially different licences**, a first here: **Menchón et al. (2018), F1000Research, CC BY 4.0** (fully remixable) for the current clinical picture, and **National Research Council (1999), *Pathological Gambling: A Critical Review*, National Academies Press** — **not openly licensed**, freely readable but copyrighted — for the DSM-III/III-R/IV criteria history, which is therefore **summarised rather than reproduced**, the handling §4 prescribes for StatPearls. A `licence_note` field on each job records which applies, so the distinction survives independently of the page. **The reclassification is the spine of the page**: DSM-5 moved gambling disorder into *Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders*, **the first behavioural addiction placed alongside the substance disorders**, where from 1980 to 1994 the same behaviour sat under *Impulse Control Disorders Not Elsewhere Classified* — a category being **re-theorised rather than discovered**, and Menchón et al. note the move also changes perceived dangerousness, expectations of recovery and attributions of responsibility. Three numbers carry it: **only ~10% of people with the disorder ever seek treatment** (so every other figure describes that tenth, selected for severity); **32% suicidal ideation and 17% lifetime attempts** among treatment-seekers; and **no approved drug anywhere**, with opioid antagonists the best-supported class at a meta-analytic **"small but significant benefit"**. The Canadian gap here is a **conflict of interest, not just missing data** — provincial governments both regulate gambling and depend on its revenue, provincial self-exclusion programmes have no equivalent in this literature, and neither source mentions industry funding of gambling research. **`suicide-and-self-harm` is now the single unwritten page across Tier A, foundations and overviews**, and at **11 inbound red links** it is the most-linked target in the corpus; Davies (2025) ch 22 is the source. (2022), *Introduction to Human Sexuality*, Open Oregon — CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with ch 17 adapted from Miller under **CC BY 4.0** and ch 16 from Walinga & Stangor’s *Introduction to Psychology – 1st Canadian Edition* (BCcampus). 13 pages: the `sexual-dysfunctions` and `paraphilic-disorders` overviews plus 11 disorder pages, taking **Lecture 7 Tier A to 5 of 5** and leaving only `gambling-disorder` (NIMH) and `suicide-and-self-harm` (Davies ch 22) unwritten. **The taxonomy’s rewrite-level flag on the paraphilic overview was correct, and the handling is the transferable part.** Chapter 16 carries four passages that must not reach a reference page — a cultural-relativism argument presenting adult–child sexual contact as normal in some societies, a relayed conflation of pedophilia with homosexuality, a claim that women in low-cut clothing are "exhibitionists in a sense", and a voyeurism prevalence that is stated (12%/4%) and then contradicted ("prevalence not known") in the same passage. **Each is named on the page as a source defect rather than reproduced or silently dropped** — dropping it leaves the next person to rediscover it from the source, reproducing it launders it — and a `source_quality_warning` field now carries the same warning at the job level. What the chapter gets right is the distinction the whole category depends on: **a paraphilia is an unusual sexual interest requiring no treatment; a paraphilic disorder distresses the person or victimises others** (Lehmiller), with **consent as the organising axis**. The strongest counter-pathologising evidence in the corpus sits here too — BDSM practitioners show *higher* wellbeing than average and **no correlation with childhood sexual assault** (Joyal). But the chapter supplies **no etiology and no treatment for any paraphilic disorder**, which is now the largest single declared gap in the corpus and an honest one. On the dysfunction side the teachable point is the threshold — six months, 75% of occasions, clinically significant distress — against headline survey figures (43% of women, 31% of men) that measure *difficulty in the past year* and apply none of it; the gap between those numbers is where the medicalisation argument lives. **Five sources in, the keyword-scan-before-planning rule paid off in the other direction**: it confirmed full coverage before any work began and correctly predicted 13 pages. (2020), *Abnormal Psychology*, University of Saskatchewan Open Press, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — compiled from OERs including a *different* Bridley & Daffin volume, OpenStax and Noba, so **every section carries its own author list and is cited accordingly**; a single whole-book citation would misattribute most of it. Canadian prevalence spliced into 12 pages: [[major-depressive-disorder]] lifetime **11.2% against 16.6% US**, but [[generalized-anxiety-disorder]] **8.7% against 5.7% — Canada higher, the opposite direction**, so the correction is not uniformly downward and cannot be applied as a rule of thumb. Three findings have no US-source equivalent at all: **Cluster B personality disorders in Quebec cost 13 years of life expectancy for men and 9 for women** (Cailhol 2017, a whole-province administrative cohort — nothing in the DSM-derived material conveys that these carry a mortality profile); **a third of Canadian adults have a panic attack in a year while 1–2% are diagnosed with panic disorder**, the cleanest demonstration available that the apprehension rather than the attack is the disorder; and **67.7% lifetime depression among sexual minorities and 72% among gender liminal people in Ontario**, the largest disparities in the corpus and from community rather than clinical samples. Service context is provincial and consequential — Ontario’s 2019 autism funding changes had families leaving the province for services, so "does it work" and "can you get it" are not separable. **Six new pages the WSU books have no equivalent for**: [[evidence-based-practice]] on the **Canadian Psychological Association’s own definition**; [[empirically-supported-treatments]] with the manualisation selection effect and the payer misuse the source says was never intended; **[[treatments-that-harm]]** (Lilienfeld 2007), which **closes the most-repeated `Needs research` line in the corpus** — every "what does not work" note now has a page to point at; [[eco-anxiety]]; and [[person-centered-therapy]], [[mindfulness-based-therapy]] and [[acceptance-and-commitment-therapy]], the last carrying one of the few explicit magnitude statements anywhere here (**moderate** improvement for anxiety and depression, Hofmann 2010). **Diathesis-stress is now stated formally**, closing a gap `integrative-model` had declared since Module 02 and which the handoff had earmarked a new text to fix — with **protective factors**, the half usually omitted, which is the frame that makes "why do most exposed people *not* develop the disorder" a proper question. **What it does not do matters too**: the book has no sleep-wake, sexual, paraphilic, substance, eating, dissociative, somatic or neurocognitive chapters, so it does not close §4’s uncovered list or unblock the three remaining overviews. Prior update: **Ten chapter overviews written; the Field Guide’s catalogue map is now 13/16.** Every overview that could be built from ingested material is built — the three that remain (`sleep-wake-disorders`, `paraphilic-disorders`, `sexual-dysfunctions`) are §4’s uncovered list in a different shape, since **all of their member pages are unwritten** and a chapter map assembled from nothing has no source. 7.4k–12.3k chars each, **zero empty sections across all ten**. Method: synthesise from the member pages and cite the module — the members are already faithful renderings carrying vetted figures, so the map is more accurate built from them than re-derived, and the citation still traces to where the content came from. **What overviews are actually for became clear by writing ten**: they put a chapter’s numbers in one table so the outliers show, and that is where the teaching value landed every time — the personality-disorder prevalence grid where two disorders were found at **0.0%** by one national survey and 6.2% and 1.8% by another; anorexia and bulimia at ~10:1 female while **binge-eating disorder is close to even**, which complicates the simple sociocultural account; **9% of US teens and adults against ~22% of Native Americans** for substance use, reported with no explanation and the clearest place in the corpus where Canadian material is a requirement rather than an enrichment; **50% of adults reporting a transient depersonalization episode** against 1–2% with the disorder. They also surfaced a pattern no single page could show: **four chapters develop their etiology on one member and apply it to the rest by assumption** (psychosis on schizophrenia, trauma on PTSD, OCD-related on OCD, somatic at class level only), and each overview now says so instead of implying a chapter-wide account that does not exist. **One wrong call, retracted the same day and recorded as run plan §10.6**: a claim that 168 markdown-style `[text](slug.md)` links across 35 pages never reached `wiki_links` and understated the graph. False — `sync_wiki_links()` parses both forms and the reader normalises `[[…]]` *into* that form so one renderer serves both; the link total was unchanged across the edit, which was the visible proof. The conversion had already been applied; it is harmless and display text is preserved, but it wrote a false rationale into 35 version notes, corrected in place afterwards. The lesson is ordering: the check that would have caught it was one query against `sync_wiki_links()`, and a corpus-wide defect nobody has noticed is more likely a misreading of the schema than a real bug. Prior update: **The colliding-update bug, which had already happened twice unnoticed.** An update proposal is a delta and the review UI merges it by concatenation — right when the delta adds sections, wrong when it restates them. The clean present state was that cleanup, not evidence the bug does not occur.
