### Module 14: the carve mismatch recurs, and the Module 11 playbook applies unchanged (2026-08-02)

**213s, 19,895 output tokens, 13 pages.** Second instance of the failure class Module 11 introduced, which is the useful part — the remedy was already written down, so this took a rename, a two-row migration and one queued run rather than a fresh decision.

**Module 14 carves by diagnostic level, then by aetiology:**

```
14.1 Clinical Presentation → Delirium / Major NCD / Mild NCD
14.2 Epidemiology          → Delirium / Major and Mild NCD / Subtypes
14.3 Etiology              → Alzheimer's / TBI / Vascular / Substance / Lewy / Frontotemporal / Parkinson's / Huntington's
```

The catalogue lists the aetiologies as separate disorders and has no row for the level constructs. So paper mode produced `major-neurocognitive-disorder` (7,669) and `mild-neurocognitive-disorder` (3,432) — real pages, no catalogue home — exactly as it produced `substance-use-disorder` from Module 11.

**Three fixes, all following precedent rather than setting new policy.**

*Naming.* The model wrote DSM long-form slugs — `neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-alzheimers-disease` and `…-due-to-traumatic-brain-injury` — where the catalogue uses `alzheimers-disease-ncd` and `traumatic-brain-injury-ncd`. Renamed with `rename_page()`, which linked both catalogue rows and reported **2 inbound links orphaned** from `major-neurocognitive-disorder`; retargeted with `edit_page()`. Renaming *after* accepting is what §8.7 requires, and it mattered again: those links did not exist until the batch went in.

*Cataloguing.* `20260802_catalogue_ncd_foundations.sql` files the two level constructs as **lecture-10 foundations**, matching the substance three. DSM-5-TR defines major and mild NCD generically — severity threshold, the six cognitive domains, the independence criterion — and applies that frame to each aetiology, so every subtype page leans on them and Tier B would misfile load-bearing material. Catalogue 128 → 130.

*The remaining gap.* **`vascular-ncd` is Tier A and still unwritten**, though the module covers it in §14.3.3 with 11 mentions. Queued as a reference run in §5. This is the recoverable kind of gap, not the `gambling-disorder` kind — worth restating because the two look identical from a coverage count and have opposite remedies.

**Lecture 10 is not close to done, and that is expected.** Six of its nine Tier A entries — ADHD, autism, conduct disorder, ODD, intellectual developmental disorder, specific learning disorder — are Module 16's material, and Module 16 runs last by design.

Live state: **170 pages with bodies**, 0 red links, 0 blue links to an empty page, 0 duplicate headings, 0 off-catalogue disorders, review queue clear. Catalogue 130 rows: Tier A **30/54**, Tier B **13/46**, foundations 13/14, overviews 0/16.

### Module 13 by direct parse: the method changes, and the hardest run becomes the best one (2026-08-02)

**The run plan flagged Module 13 as the one most likely to fail** — ten Tier A pages in a single go, against a 300s ceiling Module 11 had already come within 13 seconds of. Done by direct parse instead, it produced **13 pages, 10 of 10 Tier A, zero empty sections, zero slug misses**, and took Tier A from 30/54 to **40/54**, the largest single jump of the sprint. Lecture 11 Tier A is complete.

**What changed is where the model call happens; nothing downstream changed at all.** The run still writes an `ingest_jobs` row, still lands `kind='proposed'` versions carrying that `job_id`, and is still accepted through `review_proposal()`. Provenance, the version trail, `needs`/`annotations`, link extraction and the collision guards all ran untouched — the corpus cannot tell this run apart from a pipeline run.

**That was the thing most likely to break, and it was checked rather than assumed.** `wiki_page_provenance` joins versions on `kind='proposed'` **and** `review_status='accepted'`, then to `ingest_jobs` by `job_id`. Writing these pages with `edit_page()` would have produced `kind='accepted'` with a null `job_id` and therefore **no sources at all** under *Built from* — a licence violation for CC BY-NC-SA material, not a cosmetic gap. Verified after acceptance: `borderline-personality-disorder` reports four sources, correctly accumulating Module 13 alongside the earlier Fonagy and Shedler journal ingests.

**Why it beats the pipeline is one idea: catalogue-first instead of source-first.** Nearly every failure recorded in the gap map traces to the pipeline being one-shot and blind — the model sees a source, carves it as the source is built, and only afterwards does anyone find that the catalogue wanted a different partition. That produced the carve mismatches on substance and NCD, the slug misses, and the semantic duplication on stubs. In-session, the module and the catalogue fit in context together, so the question becomes "here are the ten slugs I must fill" rather than "here is a chapter, see what falls out". Ten of ten matched **by construction** — no renames, no orphaned links, on a module whose ten disorders had never been written.

**Format settled empirically, and the answer is a hybrid.** Against the full 1.06M-char book HTML: HTML beats `pdftotext` on structure (real `h2`/`h3`, 274 `<ul>`, the 3 genuine tables) and is the only format that **tells you where the figures are** — but it is not sufficient. Of the book's 17 images, `Table-13.1.jpg` is a **prevalence matrix for all ten personality disorders across three data sources**, and `pdftotext` does not even preserve its caption. Read natively off PDF page 11, it gave every one of the ten pages a real Epidemiology section. So: HTML for structure, native PDF for the pages its `<img>` tags point at. Module 13 cost ~15k tokens plus two vision pages against ~65k for a native paper run — better coverage at a quarter of the input. This **amends the §5 correction**: "tables are the payload" was wrong about `<table>` markup (0 in 24 disorder pages) and right about the category, in a form no text format exposes. Prose vs image is the distinction that matters, not native vs extracted.

**The table also produced the best `contested` material in the corpus.** The three sources do not merely differ, they disagree about whether the disorders are detectable: **narcissistic 0.0% (NCS-R) against 6.2% (NESARC)**, histrionic 0.0% against 1.8%, antisocial 0.6% against 3.6%. Two disorders were not found at all by one national survey. That is an epistemics lesson the textbook's prose never states, and it anchors the new `categorical-vs-dimensional-personality-models` debate page — alongside DSM-5-TR's own concession that the cluster structure "has not been consistently validated".

**One honest caveat.** `diagnosis` is annotated on nine of the ten pages: the module gives clinical pictures, not criteria lists, so no page carries the enumerated DSM-5-TR criteria. A real and consistent gap, and exactly the scoped-ask shape the student list wants.

**The ingest GUI is now free for its actual job** — student submissions of peer-reviewed papers (WP6), which wants precisely what bulk textbook ingest fought against: one unfamiliar paper, unknown structure, a proposal queue, mandatory human review. Every guard built during the sweep is *more* valuable there. One consequence to plan for: the pipeline stops being exercised by every module run, so it needs a deliberate test pass before students touch it.

Method, recipe and the two SQL traps are recorded as run plan §9. Live state: **186 pages with bodies**, 660 wikilinks, 3 red links (all pointing at real catalogue slugs not yet written — `adhd`, `conduct-disorder`, `brief-psychotic-disorder`), 0 duplicate headings, 0 off-catalogue disorders, queue clear. Catalogue 130 rows: Tier A **40/54**, Tier B 14/46, foundations 13/14, overviews 1/16. Six lectures now have complete Tier A coverage — L3, L4, L5, L9 and L11 outright, L8 at 4 of 5.

### The red set: which gaps must not be student work (2026-08-03)

**Planning WP6 (student submission) forced a triage of the 303-annotation backlog, and the useful axis
is not difficulty.** The sorting question is: *what happens if this is answered wrongly and nobody
catches it?*

| Tier | Rule | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Green** — student-owned | a wrong answer is *visibly* wrong or harmless | prevalence figures, Canadian rates, "has the field moved", policy and historical context, measurement instruments |
| **Amber** — student-drafted, staff-verified | a wrong answer is *plausible-looking* | effect sizes, characterising a contested literature, saying who disagrees with whom |
| **Red** — never student work | a wrong answer reads as **clinical instruction** or creates **compliance exposure** | dosing and tapering, consent requirements, crisis resources, forensic standards, **all licence determinations** |

**Difficulty and risk come apart, and that is the whole point.** A student could close the
benzodiazepine tapering annotation competently from a guideline in an hour. The problem is the
artefact, not the effort: a confident tapering schedule in a wiki other students read **is** clinical
guidance whatever disclaimer sits above it, and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill people. Likewise
licence determination — knowing an NIH author manuscript is free-to-read but **not** CC-licensed, and
writing the provenance row accordingly — is a compliance surface that should not be delegated.

**The red set is 11 items across 10 pages**, found by pattern-matching the annotations for dosing,
tapering, withdrawal management, consent, contraindications, antidotes, overdose, crisis resources,
mandated reporting, civil commitment, sentencing, fitness to stand trial and codes of ethics. Two are
now closed, both from **Canadian** sources.

**`sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic`** — College of Family Physicians of Canada deprescribing guideline
(Pottie et al., 2018). The finding worth carrying is an apparent contradiction that isn't one: a
**strong** recommendation to taper in adults 65+ resting on **low-quality** evidence, because the
strength derives from the **harms of continued use** rather than from trials showing deprescribing
works. **Recommendation strength is not a restatement of evidence quality.** Also: **no trials
compare tapering schedules with each other**; switching to a long-acting agent has not been shown to
help; **60–80%** stop after a deprescribing intervention against **10–20%** on usual care; withdrawal
is milder than its reputation (no overall difference in symptom scores versus continuation, and
seizures do not appear to occur *with* tapering); melatonin doesn't improve cessation; CBT's advantage
doesn't survive to 3 or 12 months. Scope caveat recorded on the page — the guideline covers people
prescribed these drugs **for insomnia**, not the misuse population its own Epidemiology section
describes.

**`opioid-use-disorder`** — CRISM national guideline (Bruneau et al., 2018, *CMAJ*).
**Buprenorphine–naloxone is first-line** (strong, high certainty), breaking with ASAM and WHO, which
had treated it and methadone as equivalent; UK data put it at **six times safer than methadone for
overdose**. The recommendation to teach is the counter-intuitive one: **withdrawal management alone
should be avoided**, because it raises relapse, transmission and overdose death — tolerance falls
faster than supply does. Psychosocial treatment is recommended **but explicitly decoupled from access
to medication**, a 2011 Cochrane review of 35 RCTs having found no added benefit for retention,
abstinence or relapse. Canadian regulatory asymmetry: **methadone needs a Health Canada exemption
everywhere; buprenorphine–naloxone does not, in most provinces** — so the safer drug is also the more
accessible one.

**New house convention.** Red-set material is written in **reporting register** — *the guideline says
X*, not *do X* — carries an explicit not-clinical-instruction note, and **states the guideline's own
scope**, because the commonest way to mislead here is not getting a fact wrong but applying a
guideline to a population it excludes.

**Also noted for WP6:** the original plan earmarked Tier B stubs as the student-contribution target.
**There are no stubs now** — all 131 catalogue pages are full articles — so the annotation becomes the
natural unit. But annotations are inline `> **Needs research:**` markers with no ID, no claim
mechanism and no status, so making them assignable is a **schema change**, not a content task.

### A contribution pipeline: gaps, precheck, and a submissions queue (2026-08-06)

**The Field Guide can now be worked on by students without a TA reading every word.** Three pieces:
`page_gaps` (what needs doing), an automated precheck (what is mechanically wrong), and
`/academic/fieldguide/submissions` (what a human still has to judge).

**The design decision: the unit is the ask, not the annotation.** Measured before building — 301
`Needs research` markers, averaging **2.39 distinct asks each**, with 215 of 301 containing more than
one, written as "X; Y; and Z". At one row per marker the pool is **301**, under half of what
200 students × 3 contributions needs. Split on asks it is **675**, plus **62** empty sections =
**737 gaps**. **That split is the thing that makes the cohort size work**, so the schema is built on
it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Green — student-owned | 134 gaps, **268 slots** (capacity 2) |
| Amber — student-drafted, staff-verified | 592 |
| Red — never student work | 11 |
| | **860 student slots against 600 required** |

Green carries capacity 2 because prevalence and rates asks legitimately take more than one source
(different populations, criteria, years) — and because 134 green gaps would not otherwise cover
200 students needing a gentle first task.

> **Corpus as of 2026-08-11: 743 gaps · 126 green · 605 amber · 12 red · 867 student slots.** The
> table above is the shape at build time; the greens moved on the 2026-08-08 difficulty adjudication,
> and six **curated** gaps were added on 2026-08-11 (`20260811_wp7_curated_gaps.sql`) by the WP7
> item-format audit. Those six matter beyond their count: **every one sits in a section that already
> holds prose**, so `extract_page_needs()` reads it as filled and `populate_page_gaps()` could never
> derive it. Writing exam questions against the guide turned out to be the only process that reads it
> the way a student under time pressure does — it found a chapter that explains antipsychotics by a
> dopamine mechanism it never states, a symptom/phase claim the corpus implies backwards, and a
> duty-to-protect question resting on doctrine the page does not carry. `kind='curated'` is the
> staff-flagging route from WP6 Phase D: recorded against the page without touching page content, so
> no flag passes through provenance.

**Two durability decisions.** Gaps key on `(page_id, ask_hash)`, so a claim is **not lost when
neighbouring prose is edited**. And `populate_page_gaps()` **never deletes** — asks that vanish from
prose surface in a `stale_gaps` view for staff to retire, because deleting would orphan claims.

**Difficulty is a triage aid, not a classification, and the failures are instructive.** The seeding
regex produced false positives in *both* directions: "the opioid crisis" matched the crisis-line
rule; "hours-per-week dose-response" matched drug dosing; and **`\yAct\y` matched *Acceptance and
Commitment Therapy*** four times. Meanwhile "Canadian reporting duties" passed as green when mandated
reporting is a legal standard. **Legal vocabulary is full of ordinary English** — anchoring terms to
their neighbours (`duty to warn`, `civil commitment`) rather than matching them alone cut false
positives from 26 to 5. A `gap_review_queue` view now surfaces only boundary cases, turning the audit
into a **17-row** job.

**The precheck exists because of arithmetic.** At 600 submissions, the irreducible human step —
opening the source and confirming it says what the student claims — is **50–100 hours a term**. Nine
checks strip the mechanical faults first: red-gap, unresolvable citation, fair-dealing quote length,
word count, the mandatory *"what this source cannot tell us"* field, duplicate sources both against the
page and against other submissions — and the sharpest, **`clinical_instruction`**, which catches the
likeliest novice failure: **answering a green lookup question and padding it with treatment advice**.
A green *gap* does not guarantee green *prose*.

**Verified with deliberate fixtures**, not by inspection. A bad submission ("modafinil 200 mg daily as
first-line treatment… patients should be titrated", a 320-character quote, 19 words, empty limitation)
raised all four planted findings **plus a duplicate-source warning nobody planted**. A well-formed one
raised a **genuine** duplicate — its DOI was already cited on `alcohol-use-disorder`. That check will
earn its keep once 200 students reach for the same obvious review article.

**`route` is the layout principle of the review page**, because a TA's scarce resource is attention:
**BLOCKED** needs no reading at all, **light check** is a green gap that passed precheck, **full read**
is everything else. **Review links land on the exact section** — `/academic/fieldguide/wiki/<slug>#<section>`,
with 666 of 737 gaps resolving to an anchor and the rest to the page top — and open in a new tab,
because losing the queue mid-review is how a reviewer loses their place.

**Partitioned per the route convention**: its own lazy route and its own **8 KB** chunk, separate from
`/review`. That one is the staff *authoring* path (ingest proposals); this is the student
*contribution* path. Different reviewers, different failure modes. Accepting a submission writes only
to `gap_claims.status` — **nothing here touches `wiki_pages`**, because a page write must carry
provenance and a claim does not supply one.

### The catalogue closes (2026-08-03)

**Six sources, four pages, and the last unwritten slug.** `sleep-wake-disorders` lost its `contested`
gap, `circadian-rhythm-sleep-wake-disorders` and `hypersomnolence-disorder` were written, and
`brief-psychotic-disorder` was taken in the same pass because it was the only thing remaining.

```
catalogue rows          131
catalogue pages written 131   (0 missing)
distinct link targets   244
targets that resolve    244   (0 red links)
```

**Red links have been a working signal since WP2. This is the first time the count is zero.** Every
slug in `disorders` has a body; every one of the corpus's 1,443 wikilinks lands on a real page.

**The finding: a remission rate is a property of the study's horizon, not of the disorder.** The two
sources on `brief-psychotic-disorder` appeared to contradict each other — Correll et al. (2008) found
**three of four** adolescents with the diagnosis fully remitted; Fusar-Poli et al. (2017) found **54%**
of 80 people with Brief Limited Intermittent Psychotic Symptoms developed a persistent psychotic
disorder. The transition curve reconciles them:

| Time from BLIPS | Transitioned |
|---|---|
| 3 months | 10% |
| 12 months | 19% |
| 24 months | 30% |
| **60 months** | **54%** |

Correll's mean follow-up was **22.8 months** — right where transition sits near 30% and is still
climbing. The studies are not in conflict; they stopped watching at different times. **This becomes a
standing question for the review pass alongside §21's "what is the newest source": over what period
was this outcome measured?** Supporting detail: 68% of the BLIPS cohort also met ICD-10 acute and
transient psychotic disorder criteria, so the two literatures are the same territory under different
names, and prior studies of this population report **diagnostic instability of 23% to 87%** — a range
wide enough to be a statement about the category rather than about the studies.

**Second finding: sleep medicine does not use the DSM, and that closed the overview's gap with an
observation rather than an argument.** Steele et al. (2021), a contemporary review of the circadian
disorders, defines all six subtypes by **ICSD-3** and never mentions DSM-5. ICD-11 places sleep-wake
disorders in **Chapter 07, outside the mental and behavioural disorders**. And the AASM hypersomnolence
guideline covers narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia and Kleine-Levin syndrome while making **no
recommendation at all for psychiatric hypersomnia** — evidence "insufficient and inconclusive" — so
the sleepiness most likely to present in a psychology clinic falls between two specialties'
guidelines. A student consulting three manuals gets three answers about whether these are psychiatric
conditions, while the specialty treating them uses a fourth book. Also recorded: DSM-5-TR's
*hypersomnolence disorder* is sleep medicine's *idiopathic hypersomnia*, so searching the DSM term
does not find the literature.

**§19.6 keeps paying, and this time the comparison is inside a single guideline.** Modafinil for
idiopathic hypersomnia rests on **1 RCT plus 4 observational studies**; modafinil for **narcolepsy**,
in the same document, rests on **9 RCTs plus 4 observational studies**. Same drug, neighbouring
disorder, nine times the evidence. The panel's own caveats are quoted on the page — small samples
throughout, older treatments "rarely evaluated using a randomized controlled trial design", and
**"comparative effectiveness studies were virtually nonexistent"** — so a recommendation table ranks
what has been *tested*, systematically disadvantaging older and cheaper drugs. Steele et al. give the
matching verdict for the circadian disorders: treatment "remains more as an **art-of-medicine
approach**" than a trial-based one.

**A teaching table worth reusing.** Light and melatonin phase-response curves run roughly **180° out
of phase**, so both treatments reverse direction depending on timing — morning light and evening
melatonin pull sleep earlier; evening light and morning melatonin push it later. A patient
self-medicating melatonin at the wrong hour moves their clock the wrong way, and effective doses
(**0.5 mg**) are far below what is sold.

**Job-row note:** Steele and Maski each served **two** target pages, so each needed **two** job rows —
one per (source, target) pair. Four jobs from two sources.

**State:** 262 pages, 1,443 wikilinks, 175 jobs, **0 red links**, **0 unwritten catalogue pages**,
major-tier gaps 9 across 8 → **8 across 7**. Empty sections 68 → 72 and annotations 300 → 303, both
rising because the three new pages carry honestly declared gaps. **Content is no longer the binding
constraint** — after the remaining eight gaps the work is the review pass and publishing.

### The Lecture 8 block, and a metric that was quietly lying (2026-08-03)

**13 sources, 8 pages, one sweep.** `substance-intoxication` went from four declared gaps to zero,
and the seven unwritten Lecture 8 catalogue slugs were written: `inhalant-use-disorder`,
`caffeine-related-disorders`, `hallucinogen-related-disorders`,
`sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic-related-disorders`, `tobacco-use-disorder`, `kleptomania`,
`pyromania`. **Unwritten catalogue pages 10 → 3; major-tier gaps 13 across 9 pages → 9 across 8.**

**The transferable finding: what a source counts is not what the page is about.** Three pages turned
on it.

| Page | What the number actually measures |
|---|---|
| `substance-intoxication` | A 1,344-case consecutive ED series is **55.7% intentional self-poisoning** — psychiatric medications (19.4%), NSAIDs (18.9%) and paracetamol (14.4%) outweigh recreational substances (21.0%) and alcohol (8.3%). Men were **92.2%** of recreational-drug cases; women **67.6%** of intentional poisonings, so the sex ratio has no single answer |
| `pyromania` | A search for the **diagnosis** returns essentially nothing. The 1.0% lifetime figure is for **fire-setting**, measured with a *single item*, and the study reports **no count of people meeting pyromania criteria at all** |
| `sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic` | When NSDUH rewrote its definition of "misuse" in 2015, reported misuse of one's own prescription moved **14.1% → 21.8%** with no change in behaviour |

Rule for the review pass: **before quoting a prevalence figure, ask what the denominator's
recruitment channel was.**

**§19.6 — state the evidence base before the findings — earned its keep three times.** The Brazilian
Psychiatric Association consensus on managing acute intoxication states that it **could not grade its
evidence at all** — not by the Oxford method, not GRADE, not AMSTAR, because "the literature is still
scarce." It used a three-round Delphi instead, and **only 52 of 102 proposed items cleared the 65%
threshold**: half of what a national specialist panel proposed could not command two-thirds agreement
among the panel. For inhalants, exactly one randomised trial exists and it addresses comorbid
psychiatric symptoms rather than the inhalant use — everything else is case reports, presented on the
page as a table with an *evidence behind it* column. **`tobacco-use-disorder` is the deliberate
opposite pole** and now serves as the corpus's contrast case: 136 trials, 64,640 participants, RR
1.55 (1.49–1.61), GRADE high, with the authors telling funders to stop running these trials.

**Two clinical inversions worth teaching.** Blood alcohol concentration does not define intoxication
— the consensus lists >400 mg/dL for respiratory depression and death *and* a lethal dose of ~300
mg/dL in a non-tolerant person, a figure sitting **below** the severe band; that is tolerance, and it
is why a tolerant drinker's overdose risk rises. And for HPPD, **risperidone is the drug theory
recommends and the drug to avoid** — it worsens the visual disturbance, probably via α2 presynaptic
antagonism. Mechanism does not substitute for outcome data.

**A measurement flaw in the tracking, found while counting.**
`reference_worklist.annotation_count` only counts annotations on pages that **still have a derived
gap**. A page that closes its last empty section drops out of the view, and its
`> **Needs research:**` markers stop being counted.

```
annotations via the worklist view:   33   (19 pages)
annotations actually in the corpus: 298  (139 pages)
```

Every annotation figure previously reported here and in the handoff — including the "watch
annotations, not just empty sections" guidance — was a **filtered subset**. The derived-gap tracking
is unaffected and remains sound; what was wrong is the impression that the backlog is small. **More
than half the corpus carries at least one in-prose research ask**, and closing the last major-tier
derived gaps will not change that.

**Two process mistakes, both caught by assertions rather than by reading.** A `replace()` whose
anchor spanned `## Contested` deleted the heading and silently absorbed the section into its
neighbour — length deltas looked fine, and only asserting on `extract_page_sections()`'s section
list caught it. And the first `kleptomania` version drew on **two sources under one `job_id`**, which
would have credited one source for both in `wiki_page_provenance`; it was rejected and rewritten as
two versions. Worth knowing for next time: **rejecting the only version of a new page returns
`page_dropped: true` and deletes the shell page**, so it has to be recreated before re-proposing.

**Canadian content.** Kirst et al. (2013), two national surveys (n = 123,846 and 13,581): problematic
alcohol and illicit drug use and mental health problems are all significantly more prevalent among
current smokers, with effects **significantly larger among youth** — and the authors' own conclusion
that "not enough is known about the prevalence of various types of tobacco use co-morbidities among
the Canadian population" is itself the citable finding. Standing annotations left on
`inhalant-use-disorder` (volatile substance use among Indigenous youth in remote and northern
communities, absent from both sources) and `tobacco-use-disorder` (Canadian prevalence, provincial
and Indigenous breakdowns).

**State:** 259 pages, 1,426 wikilinks, 169 ingest jobs, 68 empty sections, **0 off-catalogue red
links** — four introduced during the sweep were caught by the standing check and repointed.

### `alternatives-to-categorical-diagnosis`: four challengers that disagree with each other (2026-08-03)

**Why this gap and not a bigger one.** It was a single empty section, on a page with **23 inbound
wikilinks** — second only to `evidence-based-practice`. The contested sections written during the
L9–L11 sweeps had been *pointing at it*: the dimensional-vs-categorical argument on OCD severity
bands, the three-column prevalence disagreement on personality disorders, DMDD's DSM/ICD placement
split, insomnia's collapsed subtypes. Each says "see `diagnosis-and-classification`" for an argument
that was not there. **A red link is visible; a blue link to a declared gap is not.** Rank derived gaps
by inbound links, not only by tier.

**Four sources, one per item the old marker named:**

| Source | Covers | Licence |
|---|---|---|
| Krueger & Hobbs (2020), *Psychopathology* | DSM-5 Section III AMPD | NIH Public Access author manuscript — free to read, **not CC** |
| Conway et al. (2019), *Perspectives on Psych. Science* | HiTOP | NIHPA author manuscript — free to read, **not CC** |
| Cuthbert (2014), *World Psychiatry* | RDoC | © WPA, open access |
| Borsboom (2017), *World Psychiatry* | network theory | © WPA, open access |

Two are **author manuscripts, not CC-licensed** — readable and citable under the NIH policy, but not
an open licence, and the provenance rows say so rather than claiming one the source doesn't carry.

**The finding the section is built around: "the dimensional alternative" is not one position.** DSM
categories, the AMPD's traits and HiTOP's spectra all keep the **common-cause / latent-variable**
model — something hidden generates the symptoms — and argue only about its shape; RDoC relocates it to
neural circuitry. **Borsboom's network theory removes it**: symptoms cause each other, and the
pathology *is* the set of interactions. That matters for teaching, because HiTOP and network models
are routinely presented as allies against the DSM while resting on incompatible premises — Conway et
al. concede only that they are "not necessarily mutually exclusive". The section closes on a five-row
table whose "why symptoms co-occur" column is where the fault line shows.

**Second finding: none of the four can yet do the DSM's job, and each says so.** RDoC is not a
diagnostic system *by design*; HiTOP awaits normative data and agreed cutoffs — the same practical
thresholds it faults the DSM for setting arbitrarily; network theory has no trial showing
network-guided treatment beats standard care. So the categorical model is **less defended by the
evidence than left standing by the absence of a deployable replacement**, and `## Contested` now says
that rather than implying a consensus that doesn't exist.

**A debt that lived in prose, where no tool could see it.** `## How reliable is a diagnosis?` had
ended by noting the textbook gives no kappa values, so the figure "has to be sourced elsewhere". That
sentence *was* prose, so `extract_page_needs()` tracked nothing. The HiTOP source supplied it —
**roughly 40% of diagnoses examined in the DSM-5 field trials fell short of acceptable inter-rater
agreement** — recorded with the qualification that it is a secondary characterisation offered while
arguing for an alternative classification, not the primary trial report. This is the §21 lesson in a
second form: there, a stale section had no declared gap; here, a declared debt sat somewhere the
tooling cannot look. **Read the prose of sections you are already sourcing.**

**One source, two pages.** `personality-disorders` carried an annotation asking for precisely "the
AMPD and why it was not adopted as primary". A second job row against that target slug closed it, and
the answer is worth stating: **the reasons were political, and the model's authors say so** — the work
"proved to be fraught with political and practical complexities", the compromise was to print both
models, and the resistance came from psychiatry's need to "preserve the tradition of the medical model
as a basis for ensuring putative legitimacy". Corroborating detail: most AMPD research appears in
psychology journals, not psychiatry journals. **ICD-11 made the opposite call** — types abolished,
severity rating mandatory — so on personality the two manuals this corpus elsewhere calls *converging*
have in fact diverged.

**A mistake worth recording.** Building the section in four provenance-separated increments, step 3
replaced an anchor spanning `## Contested` with text that did not restore the heading. The section was
silently absorbed into its neighbour; nothing errored, and the character-count delta looked correct
because the inserted block dwarfed the 12 characters lost. What caught it was asserting on
`extract_page_sections()`'s section *list*, where `contested` had simply vanished. **When a
replacement spans a heading, assert on the section list, not the length.** The bad version was
rejected rather than patched, so the page history shows one clean accept per source.

**State:** `diagnosis-and-classification` 16.4k → 37.1k chars, 8 sections, **zero gaps**, five sources
in provenance. Major-tier gaps **14 across 10 pages → 13 across 9**; empty sections 65 → 64.

### Field Guide signup sent everyone to localhost (2026-08-03)

**Reported from a real signup attempt: the confirmation email linked to `localhost`.** Two causes, one
in code and one in configuration.

**The code half.** `FieldGuideAuthRoute` called `client.auth.signUp({ email, password })` with **no
`emailRedirectTo`** — unlike `Signup.jsx` and `ForgotPassword.jsx`, which both pass
`window.location.origin`. With no `redirectTo`, Supabase falls back to the project’s **Site URL**, and
the radlab-academic project’s is still a development URL. Signup now redirects to
`/academic/fieldguide/wiki`, which is under the guard — so the guard creates the course client, the
client consumes the token in the URL, and its `onAuthStateChange` subscription re-renders signed in.

**A second hazard found while fixing it, which would have broken the link even once redirected.** The
Field Guide authenticates against a **different Supabase project**, but `src/lib/supabase.js` creates
the main-site client with `detectSessionInUrl` on by default. A confirmation link landing under
`/academic/…` carries a token the main project cannot use — and the main client would have tried to
consume it anyway, either writing another project’s session into this one’s storage or eating a
single-use code before the academic client could exchange it. Detection is now disabled **only** on
`/academic` paths; the main site’s own `/verified` and `/reset-password` flows still depend on it.

**The configuration half is not in this repo and has to be set in the dashboard.** Supabase ignores
`emailRedirectTo` unless the URL is on the project’s **Redirect URLs** allow-list — their own
troubleshooting page, *"Why am I being redirected to the wrong url when using auth redirectTo
option?"*, says exactly this. So on the **radlab-academic** project, Authentication → URL
Configuration needs **Site URL `https://radlab.zone`** and **`https://radlab.zone/**`** on the
redirect allow-list. **Until that is set, the code fix alone will not work** — the link will keep
falling back to Site URL.

### Card view: the chapter icons become the browse (2026-08-03)

**The icons were doing too little.** At 46px beside a heading they were decoration; the browse was still
twenty stacked bands. The index now opens on a **grid of chapter cards with 96px icons**, the chapter
title, and its coverage count — twenty diagnostic classes as roughly one screen.

**Three controls, and what each is for:**

| Control | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Cards / List** segmented toggle | switches browse mode; Cards is the default |
| **Collapse all / Expand all** | **list view only** — folding means nothing until the pages are on screen |
| **Clicking a chapter card** | the bridge: switches to **list**, folds **every other** chapter, and **scrolls to** the one clicked |

**That last one is the design decision.** Opening a chapter in place would need the card grid to grow a
nested list inside one cell; landing in list view with all twenty chapters expanded would bury the
chapter that was just asked for. Switching to list with exactly one chapter open does what the click
meant.

**Two details that came out of mocking it against the real artwork** rather than reasoning about it:

- **Counts are pushed to the bottom of each card** (`margin-top: auto`), because chapter titles wrap to
  one, two or three lines and the counts otherwise sit at three different heights across a row.
- **Foundations shows no number badge.** It carries no DSM chapter number, and a placeholder dash read
  as a missing value rather than an absent one.

**One judgement call left as it was.** Switching to List from the toggle still opens with **everything
expanded** rather than everything folded — find-in-page cannot see unmounted content, so an index that
opens closed hides what it is for. Collapse all is one click away, and a card click gives the focused
view. Worth flipping if the twenty-chapter wall proves worse in use than the loss of Ctrl-F.

### *Smith v Jones* closes the duty-to-warn gap (2026-08-03)

**The entry below records this as the one thing that could not be sourced. Norm supplied the CanLII
PDF, so it is now written from the judgment itself** — placed in the duty-to-warn section beside
*Tarasoff*, where the contrast reads, rather than in the Canadian section.

**The permission-versus-duty point is anchored in the procedural history, which is stronger than
asserting it:**

| Stage | Order |
|---|---|
| Trial judge | psychiatrist was under a **duty** to disclose to police and Crown |
| Court of Appeal | varied to an order **permitting** disclosure |
| **Supreme Court** | **appeal dismissed, Court of Appeal affirmed** |

So the Canadian rule is what a clinician **may** do, where *Tarasoff* is what a Californian clinician
**must** do. Not a technicality — it moves where the professional's liability and discretion sit.

**A second difference the page now makes explicit.** *Smith v Jones* is decided as a **solicitor-client
privilege** case: the psychiatrist had been retained by defence counsel, and both parties argued it on
that footing. The Court calls that privilege **"the highest privilege recognized by the courts"**,
subject to limited exceptions of which public safety is one. *Tarasoff* arose from a **therapeutic**
relationship and a negligence claim. The two doctrines have different parents, which is why they impose
different things.

**The three factors, with the Court's own qualifications** — the qualifications being the part usually
lost in summary:

- **Clarity** — a clear risk to an **identifiable person or group**, who must be **ascertainable**. A
  general threat to everyone in a city, or anyone the person meets, **may be too vague** — but a large
  group can still qualify if clearly identified.
- **Seriousness** — the intended victim must be in danger of **death or serious bodily harm**.
- **Imminence** — the threat must create **a sense of urgency**. It **may apply to some time in the
  future**, and **no particular time limit need be imposed**.

They are **weighted, not counted**: the Court is explicit that the factors "must be defined in the
context of each situation". And where the test is met, **disclosure is still bounded** — limited to
"only the information necessary to protect public safety".

**The dissent is on the page as well**, because it makes the clinical argument the majority does not.
Lamer C.J., Major and Binnie JJ. agreed some warning was justified but would have required the breach
to be **as narrow as possible**: disclose the **opinion and that it rests on a consultation**, not the
accused's own account of the offence, which risks becoming **conscriptive evidence** against him. Their
reasoning is itself a public-safety argument — a narrow exception **"will foster a climate in which
dangerous individuals are more likely to disclose their disorders, seek treatment and pose less danger
to the public"**, and this accused **was only diagnosed and offered treatment because he felt secure in
confiding**. That is the strongest available statement of the cost side of any duty-to-warn rule, and
it comes from within the Court that created the Canadian exception.

**The divergence from *Tarasoff* is deliberate, not accidental**: the Court **considered *Tarasoff***
directly, alongside *Thompson v. County of Alameda*, *Brady v. Hopper* and the English *W. v. Egdell*.

**Handling.** A **primary legal source, not a licensed article** — a public judgment of the Supreme
Court of Canada, used by paraphrase and short quotation; the page does not reproduce it. Facts are kept
at **headnote level**: the page states the category of threat and the identified victim group, because
both are load-bearing for the clarity factor, and no method detail. Recorded in
`result_json.editorial_note`.

`law-and-ethics` is now **25,225 characters, four sources, no declared gaps**. Still open on it:
provincial **Mental Health Acts** and Ontario's **Form 1**, **fitness to stand trial** under Canadian
law, and the general (non-forensic) practice codes.

### Canadian law on `law-and-ethics`, and a source that could not be obtained (2026-08-03)

**Both declared gaps on the foundation page are closed** — `canadian-law-and-other-jurisdictions` and
`professional-ethics-codes-and-boundaries`. The page is now **21,025 characters, three sources, no
declared gaps**. But the piece it still needs is recorded prominently rather than quietly closed.

**The search finding first: the requested article does not exist where we look.** No Canada-versus-US
comparative paper turned up across NCRMD, forensic psychiatry, civil commitment, duty to warn, insanity
defence, mental health law or health-system comparison. That scholarship is in **law journals not
indexed by PubMed or Europe PMC**. The near-miss is instructive — *"Cross-Cultural Notions of Risk and
Liberty: A Comparison of Involuntary Psychiatric Hospitalization…"* compares **New York and Zurich**;
Canada appears nowhere. **Fetch before assuming from a title**, on the search side as much as the
citation side.

**Canadian primary sources were used instead**, which suits a Canadian course better than a comparison
would: the page states Canadian law directly, and the US material already there supplies the contrast.

**Section 16 of the *Criminal Code*** replaced the insanity verdict in 1992, and **Canada has no "guilty
but mentally ill" verdict**. The structural difference is what follows: a **Review Board** operating
under federal provisions but **provincially administered**, reviewing at least yearly, with detention,
conditional discharge or absolute discharge.

**The National Trajectory Project — 1,800 people found NCRMD across Quebec, Ontario and BC — runs
against the public image of the verdict:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Homicide and attempted murder | **under 7%** of all NCRMD verdicts |
| Largest categories | threats **27.4%**, assaults **26.5%** |
| Victims who were family or partners | **33.7%** (strangers **22.7%**) |
| For homicide specifically | **60.8%** family or partners |
| Psychotic-spectrum diagnosis | **70.9%** |
| Prior psychiatric hospitalisation | **72%** |

This is mostly people with psychosis, already known to services, who threatened or assaulted someone
close to them — a different clinical and policy problem from the one the insanity defence is usually
debated as being about.

**Provincial variation is large and the authors decline to explain it** — Quebec has the highest verdict
rate and the *lowest* median offence severity, Ontario the highest homicide proportion. The records
themselves differ in completeness (education missing from **44.1%** of Quebec files against **5.4%** in
BC). **A national figure conceals three systems.**

**Forensic ethics is a different ethics.** The Canadian Academy of Psychiatry and the Law guidelines
supply a role separation the page had not made: the forensic assessor is **not** the treating clinician
and must be **objective and independent of the retaining party**. And **consent inverts** — the
requirement is to explain the reason for the assessment, the assessor's role, and **the limits to
confidentiality** before beginning, because the person assessed is often not the client and the usual
promise does not hold.

**What could not be sourced, and was not faked.** **CanLII returns 403 to automated fetches**, so
***Smith v Jones* (1999 SCC)** has no source in the corpus and was **not written from memory**. The page
declares the gap and now names it as the single most important correction outstanding: *Smith v Jones*
framed disclosure as a public-safety **exception to privilege** on a three-part test — a **permission**
to disclose — against the affirmative **duty** to warn that *Tarasoff* imposed. **The CAPL guidelines
cannot close it either**: they explicitly decline to address duty to warn and **cite no Canadian case
law at all**, which the page records so a future session knows the obvious document is not the answer.

**A correction to an earlier entry.** This page was previously described here as documenting a
California decision as the duty-to-warn rule in a way that would mislead a Toronto student. That was too
strong: it **already carried a detailed Needs-research block** naming the Canadian counterparts,
including the *Smith v Jones* distinction. A declared gap, not a silent error.

### The paraphilias close: a null result reorganises the chapter (2026-08-03)

**Six pages across Lecture 7**, including both Tier A pages and the chapter overview. Major-tier gaps
**21 → 16**; `treatment` **18 → 11**; `etiology` **15 → 11**. This was the cluster flagged as having
the worst existing content — its material came from a source with documented defects — so the point was
as much to **displace** that content as to add to it.

| Page | Closed | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `pedophilic-disorder` | etiology, treatment | Joyal 2023; Landgren et al. 2022, *Drugs* |
| `paraphilic-disorders` | etiology, treatment | Joyal 2023; Culos et al. 2024, *J Clin Med* |
| `exhibitionistic-disorder`, `voyeuristic-disorder`, `fetishistic-disorder`, `sexual-sadism-and-masochism-disorders` | treatment | Culos et al. 2024 |

**The organising finding is a null result.** A neuroimaging meta-analysis of **436 men with pedophilic
disorder against 449 controls found no structural brain difference**. Pedophilic disorder is the
most-researched paraphilia by a wide margin, so a null there is the strongest available statement about
the chapter — and it means the three circulating models (**frontal-dysexecutive**, **temporal-limbic**,
**dual-dysfunction**) explain **hypersexuality and disinhibition** while **none explains the paraphilic
interest itself**. That distinction — *why someone acts* versus *why someone wants* — now runs through
the chapter.

**Acquired cases argue against the models they are usually cited to support.** Sixty-four documented
cases: 63 male, mean onset **52.8**, **81% with no premorbid interest**. They arrive with hyperphagia,
kleptomania, aggression and compulsivity — a **general failure of behavioural filtering**, sometimes
without corresponding sexual fantasies at all. A lesion that removes inhibition tells you about
inhibition; it does not tell you where a sexual preference came from. One observation is recorded as
unresolved: **almost all 64 were male**, though generalised fronto-temporal disinhibition should not be
sex-specific.

**The treatment sections open with what the evidence does not show**, because the review does.
Testosterone-lowering drugs reduce sexual *activity* — and *"it remains to be explored if reduced sexual
activity translates into a reduction in criminal sexual behavior"*, with **risk of offending not
assessed in any of the randomised trials**. Median sample **13.5**, median follow-up **15 weeks**, one
study after 2010. Harms are not incidental: **two cases of increased suicidal ideation** on degarelix,
88% injection-site reactions, 44% raised liver enzymes; **cyproterone under European restriction over
meningioma risk**. And **adding psychotherapy has not been shown to add anything on this evidence** —
drug alone versus imaginal desensitisation alone versus both produced **no significant differences**,
which is worth holding against the overview's summary that combined treatment is superior.

**Every paraphilia page states the size of the literature before naming a drug**: the whole
pharmacological base for the chapter is **28 studies and 379 people**, of which **only three of 28
scored above 5** on the Newcastle-Ottawa scale. The most-quoted recidivism figure in the field — 18% on
medroxyprogesterone, 35% after discontinuation, 58% untreated — **rests on a single 1992 study**, and
is on the page with that attached.

**Two asymmetries the sources ignore are now named on the pages.**

- `sexual-sadism-and-masochism-disorders` is **two different treatment questions**: masochism requires
  **distress in the person themselves**, sadism centres on **acting on urges with a non-consenting
  person**. A drug literature built around drive reduction and recidivism was assembled for the second
  and is routinely read onto the first.
- `fetishistic-disorder` is **the one paraphilia where the conditioning account has been studied**, so a
  learning account predicts **behavioural treatment is where the leverage is** — recorded as a gap
  rather than filled with drug evidence that answers a different question.

**Two scope decisions.** The **WFSBP guideline usually cited for this chapter is adolescent-specific**;
it was fetched, read, and deliberately **not** used as general treatment guidance — but it explains why
the field looks like this: **ethical constraints make placebo-controlled or no-treatment designs very
difficult in potential offenders**. And **prevention services are named because they are protective
information** — the German **Dunkelfeld Project**, **Stop It Now** (UK and US), the Swedish
**Preventell** helpline, **Don't Offend India** — with the review's own caveat that this literature
**includes few voluntary participants** and so generalises poorly outside forensic settings.

**Handling.** All four sources are clinical or forensic reviews, used for **etiology, treatment and
prevention only**. No offence detail appears on any page, and the decision is recorded in
`result_json.editorial_note` so it is not silently reversed.

Live state: **252 pages**, 1,383 wikilinks, 10 red links all to real catalogue slugs, queue clear,
146 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Remaining in Lecture 7: `transvestic-disorder` (absent from the
pharmacological review entirely, so it needs its own search), `exhibitionistic-disorder` etiology,
`fetishistic-disorder` epidemiology, and `contested` on the two sexual-dysfunction pages.

### Chapter icons (2026-08-03)

**One watercolour glyph per DSM-5-TR diagnostic class**, in the index chapter headings and the article
breadcrumb — a visual answer to "which chapter am I in?".

**The slicing is the part worth recording.** The set arrived as a single 2048×2048 composite with the
icons in a 4×5 grid and a caption under each. A first pass estimated the tile coordinates by eye and
**drifted far enough by the bottom-right corner to cut the artwork in half**. Decoding the PNG in Node
(zlib plus the five scanline filters — no image library is installed) and taking **ink profiles** gave
the geometry exactly:

| | |
|---|---|
| Tile box | **310 × 318** |
| Column origins | **101, 485, 869, 1253, 1637** |
| Row origins | **101, 571, 1063, 1603** |

**Columns had to be measured inside each icon row.** Measured over the whole image, a column band
includes the caption beneath the tile — and captions like "Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct
Disorders" are wider than the box they describe, so the bands came out inconsistent (310–324 px)
until the profile was restricted to an icon row's y-range, at which point every box measured 310.

**Two quirks of the supplied grid**, both handled rather than worked around: it **duplicates
"Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders"** at positions 15 and 16 — identical artwork, so
the second is skipped — and it has **no tile for chapter 20, *Other Mental Disorders***, which this
course omits anyway. That yields **19 icons for chapters 1–19**.

Sliced with **ffmpeg** — note that `convert` on PATH here is **Windows' FAT-to-NTFS converter**, not
ImageMagick — inset 3px to drop the tile border, taken as a centred 304×304 square so the scale to
192px doesn't squash it. **~2.6 KB each, 50 KB for the whole set.**

**Files register themselves.** `chapterIcons.js` globs
`src/assets/chapter-icons/<chapter number>.<name>.webp`; there is no manifest to keep in step, which
matters because the set arrived incrementally. **A chapter with no file renders no icon rather than a
broken image**, so a partial set degrades to the text-only layout it replaces.

**One build detail that would otherwise have been invisible.** Most of these icons fall under Vite's
4 KB inline threshold, so by default **16 of the 19 were base64-encoded into a shared chunk** — 56 KB
that *every* wiki page had to download, including an article page that displays exactly one 22px icon.
Setting `query: '?no-inline&url'` on the glob forces separate files: the shared chunk drops to **5.5 KB
of URLs**, the browser fetches only the icons on screen, and `loading="lazy"` starts doing something.

Icons are marked `alt="" aria-hidden` — the chapter is named in text right beside them, so a label
would only make a screen reader say it twice.

**Foundations gets one too.** The framing group carries no DSM chapter number, so it is keyed as
**chapter 0** — a real key, not a sentinel, which made one guard load-bearing: `Number(null)` and
`Number('')` are both **0**, so without an explicit empty check any page with no chapter would have
been handed the Foundations pillar. Its source art has generous margins, so
`scripts/dsm-icon-trim.mjs` crops to the content bounding box and re-emits square before scaling —
otherwise a piece of art that does not fill its frame reads smaller than the flat glyphs beside it.

**Sized at 46px in the index headings and 30px in the breadcrumb**, which is large enough to work as a
chapter marker rather than as decoration next to 20px and 13px text.

### Collapsible sections: chapter groups on the index, `##` sections on the page (2026-08-03)

**Pages outgrew the scroll.** The reference pages now run 8,000-20,000 characters with six to eleven
`##` sections, so every section folds from its own heading, with **Collapse all / Expand all** and an
"*n* of *m* folded" count above the body.

**The fold itself is trivial; the anchors are not.** Section bodies are rendered as *slices* of the
page, and `react-markdown` reports line numbers relative to whatever string it is handed. A slice
would therefore hand its headings the ids belonging to the **top of the page** — silently breaking
every table-of-contents link and every inbound `[[page#section]]`. Three things prevent that:

- `splitSections()` returns a **`startLine`** with each slice, and `WikiMarkdown` takes it as a
  **`lineOffset`**, so anchors resolve against ids computed once over the whole body.
- **Leading blank lines are stripped and the offset moves with them.** That is the off-by-one that
  would otherwise put every anchor inside a section one line short.
- **Section ids come from `extractHeadings()`, not from re-slugifying the heading text**, because that
  function **de-duplicates repeated headings** (`presentation`, `presentation-2`) — and real pages do
  repeat the six-section skeleton, `major-depressive-disorder` three times over.

**Navigation opens what it points at.** Clicking a folded section in the contents, or arriving on a
`#section` deep link, **unfolds the section that owns the anchor and scrolls on the next frame**. That
includes a `###` nested inside a folded `##`, which is why each section carries the list of anchor ids
it contains rather than just its own. The reveal also runs on the contents click itself, because a
same-page hash that hasn't changed doesn't re-fire the effect — without it, clicking a folded section
twice does nothing the second time.

**Fold state is stamped with its slug**, the same idiom `loaded` already uses for the page row, so
navigating to another page starts unfolded without an effect having to reset it and folds never leak
between pages.

**Everything starts expanded, deliberately.** Find-in-page cannot see unmounted text, and a reference
wiki that opened folded would hide the thing it was opened for. Folding is something the reader chooses;
collapsed sections are then unmounted rather than merely hidden, which keeps a 20,000-character page
from rendering markdown nobody is reading.

**Accessibility and outline are preserved:** the `<h2>` keeps the anchor id and the document outline,
and a `<button aria-expanded aria-controls>` inside it takes the click — so the heading is still a
heading to a screen reader, and the control is still a control.

**Verified before shipping**, against a real page plus synthetic cases covering an H1 preamble,
duplicate `##` *and* `###` headings, a `##` inside a fenced code block, a page with no `##` at all, and
an empty body. The checks that matter: **section ids match the table of contents, every heading inside
a slice resolves to the id the contents links to, no content line is lost, and every anchor is owned by
a section or the preamble.**

**The index folds too, and it is the one that was actually asked for.** `/academic/fieldguide/wiki`
groups the catalogue into **twenty DSM diagnostic classes**, each an `<h2>` — a long scroll to reach
the one you want. Those chapter headings now fold, with the same Collapse all / Expand all control
beside the "show unwritten entries" checkbox. **Folds are keyed by DSM chapter number, not by
position**, because flipping that checkbox changes which groups are visible; keyed by index, it would
fold a different chapter than the one clicked.

The two are separate components — `WikiIndex.jsx` folds chapter groups, `WikiPage.jsx` folds `##`
sections — and only the second has the anchor problem above, because only the second renders slices of
markdown.

### Lecture 10 goes clear, and a deliberately-omitted chapter gets a page (2026-08-03)

**`communication-disorders`** was the last multi-gap page in Lecture 10. Four CC BY sources closed
**epidemiology, etiology, treatment and contested**; the page is now 19,215 chars with five sources and
**zero declared gaps**.

| Section | Source |
|---|---|
| epidemiology | Calder et al. 2022, *J Paediatr Child Health* (Raine Study birth cohort) |
| etiology | Mountford et al. 2022, *Children* |
| treatment | Rinaldi et al. 2021, *Brain Sciences* |
| contested | Sansavini et al. 2021, *Brain Sciences* |

**Ascertainment decides the answer, twice on one page.** Heritability of developmental language
disorder is **0.97 in clinically ascertained twins and near zero in population-screened twins**. And
the long-standing claim that the disorder is commoner in boys **disappears in an unselected cohort** —
**52.9% male, p = 0.799** — which the authors attribute to **referral bias toward males and
under-detection of females**. A sex ratio drawn from clinic samples measures who gets referred, not who
is affected.

**Only 2 of the 104 children meeting criteria had ever been identified by a health professional.** Set
that against the diagnostic review's conclusion that there is **insufficient evidence to introduce
universal screening** — no screening age or tool outperformed any other — and the tension is the
teachable part rather than something to resolve.

**The treatment evidence runs the wrong way relative to the epidemiology.** Expressive targets have RCT
support (expressive phonology SMD 0.44-0.74, morphosyntax 1.02, vocabulary 1.08 against no
intervention). **Receptive vocabulary has no studies at all** — while **46.2%** of affected children
have combined receptive-expressive difficulties and 20.2% are receptive-only. And the one long
follow-up (Wake et al.) found the experimental group's gains **gone by age 6 with controls caught up**,
which suggests intervention **accelerated development rather than changing the outcome**.

**The nosology limits the genetics.** Genetic studies used language cutoffs from **1.25 to 2.0 SD**
with inconsistent non-verbal IQ thresholds, which the review attributes to the **absence of
international diagnostic consensus**. Samples that are not the same cannot be pooled; results that are
not comparable cannot replicate. FOXP2 is the famous gene and accounts for **about 2% of childhood
apraxia of speech** and nothing else; GWAS variants sit at odds ratios near 1.1. The review also states
that gene-gene interaction, gene-environment interaction and epigenetics are each **very likely to
matter and none has been demonstrated** — an unusually clean statement of a field's confidence
exceeding its data.

**And elimination disorders now has a page.** It existed nowhere in the corpus — no page, no catalogue
row — and that was **not an oversight**: `dsm_chapters` records **Chapter 11 as `taught = false`**,
one of only two chapters so marked (with Ch. 20, *Other Mental Disorders*). The decision was on the
record; the effect was that an entire DSM chapter was invisible.

It is now written as an **explicitly out-of-scope overview** — the opening section states that the
course does not teach it, that it is not exam material, and that it is deliberately thinner than a
taught page. Catalogued with **`tier = 'overview'` and `lecture = NULL`** (catalogue rows 130 → 131),
which is the honest encoding: the page exists, no lecture teaches it.

**Its justification is the comorbidity, which is the part a psychology course would actually use.**
**20-30% of children with enuresis and 30-50% of those with encopresis** carry a clinically relevant
comorbid disorder — **over a fourfold increase** on peers, [[adhd]] most frequent. Where effects reach
significance they are mostly **externalising**: attention problems (0.37), social problems (0.39),
self-concept (0.42), aggression (0.33). **Depression and anxiety do not differ significantly**, which
is the surprising result and the one worth teaching. Causal direction is unresolved — the review sets
out four non-exclusive explanations and notes that almost every study is cross-sectional. **Encopresis
is left as a declared gap**: 7 studies of 214 children against 32 of 3,244 for enuresis, and the page
says so rather than padding.

**The rule both pages produced:** where a page covers less than its title claims, **repeat the scope
limit in the section that carries the numbers**, not only in a note at the top. `communication-disorders`
states its language-disorder-only scope in Epidemiology — where a reader is most likely to lift a
figure — and again at the end of Contested. A scope note at the head of a long page is read once and
then forgotten.

Live state: **252 pages with bodies**, 1,361 wikilinks, 10 red links all to real catalogue slugs, 0
duplicate headings, queue clear, **131 catalogue rows**, 138 ingest jobs, **0 published**.

### The neurocognitive chapter closes: the first complete DSM chapter (2026-08-03)

**Thirteen pages, zero declared gaps.** DSM-5-TR Chapter 17 is the first chapter in the corpus where
every page has every section filled. Four more sources finished it — Outeiro et al. (2019) for Lewy
body pathogenesis and Parkinson's disease dementia, Jurcau et al. (2024) for prion disease, Anderson et
al. (2018) for Huntington's, Vastag et al. (2022) for HIV — including the last unwritten catalogue page
in the chapter.

**A composite page can define its own section scheme.**
`neurocognitive-disorder-other-aetiologies` is one catalogue slug covering **four unrelated diseases**
— Parkinson's, Huntington's, HIV and prion disease. Forcing them through the standard
Presentation/Diagnosis/Epidemiology/Etiology/Treatment/Contested scheme would have produced six sections
of four disconnected paragraphs each. It uses `##` headings **per disease** instead — and the gap
machinery works *better* that way, because `extract_page_sections()` keys on **any** `##` heading.
Before the diseases were written, the page's `needs` read:

```
hiv-associated-neurocognitive-disorder | huntingtons-disease |
parkinsons-disease-dementia | what-is-contested-across-these-four
```

Each unwritten aetiology surfaced as its own named gap and closed independently. **The standard six are
a default for single-disorder pages, not a schema.**

**A four-source page needs four sequential versions.** Provenance joins version → job, so the page was
created with the prion section written and the other three as explicit
`> **Needs research:** not yet written from a source.` placeholders; each later version replaced
exactly one. Every intermediate state declared precisely what was missing, and the finished page carries
**4 sources** under *Built from* rather than attributing everything to one job.

**The finding the chapter kept producing — now visible because the pages sit next to each other:
removing the pathological protein has failed to help in three separate diseases.**

| Disease | Intervention | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Prion disease | **PRN100** anti-PrP antibody | **cleared the abnormal protein**, no effect on clinical progression |
| Alzheimer's disease | lecanemab, donanemab | amyloid cleared; differences **below the threshold of perception** |
| Lewy body disease | — | **Lewy body density does not correlate** with duration, onset, fluctuations, hallucinations, delusions, falls, parkinsonism or cognitive decline |

Either the visible aggregate is not the toxic agent in any of them, or by the time it is visible the
damage is done. The Lewy body literature has the sharpest version: *in vitro*, **fibril uptake is
associated with a protective outcome** while **monomer and oligomer uptake triggers apoptosis** — which
would make the structure the disease is named after the brain's **defence**.

**And certainty about cause buys less than a course might expect.** Huntington's disease has a single
identified autosomal dominant mutation, testable years before onset — and its neuropsychiatric
management rests on **expert consensus**, because there are *"insufficient data for evidence-based
guidelines."* Prion disease is understood in molecular detail and **every therapeutic attempt has
failed**.

**Four more things worth teaching from these pages:**

- **Two dementias separated by a stopwatch.** DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia are distinguished by
  the **one-year rule** — which symptom set was noticed first — on a boundary its own authors call
  arbitrary, with **end-stage neuropathology that may be identical**.
- **Criteria that manufacture cases.** The **Frascati criteria** put the HAND cutoff at 1 SD across
  multiple domains, and **15-22% of people without HIV test positive** on extensive batteries.
  Antiretroviral therapy left **overall prevalence steady at 30-60%** while shifting nearly all of it to
  the asymptomatic end (HIV-associated dementia **2%** in CHARTER).
- **Check the drug before treating the symptom.** The Huntington guidance for apathy says to **reduce
  SSRIs and neuroleptics first** — apathy caused by an SSRI is indistinguishable from apathy caused by
  the disease. Similarly, anxiety is routinely confused with **akathisia**.
- **In rapidly progressive dementia the expensive error is missing the reversible mimic** — autoimmune
  encephalitis (responds well to immunotherapy, antibodies **initially negative in up to 50%**),
  lithium toxicity, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, and **thiamine deficiency, whose MRI can show
  the same cortical ribboning as CJD**.

Live state: **251 pages with bodies**, 1,353 wikilinks, 10 red links all to real catalogue slugs, 0
duplicate headings, queue clear, 132 ingest jobs, **0 published**.

### The Lecture 10 sweep, and a class of error the gap query cannot see (2026-08-03)

**Nine sources, eight pages, two of them new.** `treatment` gaps fell **23 → 18**, and every page in
the neurocognitive chapter except `neurocognitive-disorder-other-aetiologies` now has a treatment
section.

| Page | Source | Closed |
|---|---|---|
| `neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-alzheimers-disease` | Espay, Kepp & Herrup 2024, *eNeuro*; Haass & Selkoe 2022, *PLoS Biology* | **stale treatment replaced**; contested enriched |
| `delirium` | Abraha et al. 2015, *PLOS ONE* | treatment |
| **`neurocognitive-disorder-with-lewy-bodies`** *(new)* | McKeith et al. 2017, *Neurology* | whole page bar etiology |
| `frontotemporal-neurocognitive-disorder` | Gambogi et al. 2021 | treatment, contested |
| `mild-neurocognitive-disorder` | Chen et al. 2021, *Front Neurol* | treatment |
| `vascular-neurocognitive-disorder` | Jaul & Meiron 2017 | treatment |
| `neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-traumatic-brain-injury` | Barman et al. 2016 | treatment |
| **`substance-medication-induced-neurocognitive-disorder`** *(new)* | Sachdeva et al. 2016; Wijnia 2022 | whole page |

**The methodological finding is the one worth carrying forward: a page can be complete, declare no
gaps, and still be wrong.** `neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-alzheimers-disease` had a full treatment
section citing the Alzheimer's Association, **2017**, and a sentence describing disease-modifying
approaches as **"research in its infancy."** That was true when written. By 2026 **lecanemab and
donanemab had completed phase 3 and reached clinical use, and neither appeared on the page.**

**The gap query cannot find this.** `needs` and `annotations` surface only what a page *declares*
missing; a confidently-written stale section declares nothing. This one was found by reading the
treatment section while checking something unrelated. **The standing check that follows: for every
page, what is the newest source, and has the field moved since?** Treatment sections and citations to
advocacy organisations rather than journals are the exposed cases — presentation ages slowly,
treatment does not.

**The replacement is the corpus's cleanest demonstration of relative-versus-absolute framing.**

| | Lecanemab | Donanemab |
|---|---|---|
| Difference from placebo | **0.45** points (CDR-SB, 18-point scale) | **3.4** points (iADRS, 144-point scale) |
| Reported as | "27% slowing" | "33% slowing" |
| Share of the whole scale | **2.5%** | **2.4%** |
| Minimal clinically important difference | 1.0 / 1.6 | 5 / 9 |
| **Below MCID?** | **yes, both** | **yes, both** |
| Treatment-related adverse events | 45% | 89% |
| Brain swelling and/or bleeding | ~25% | >33% |
| **Number needed to harm** | **~3** | **~3** |

Both framings describe the same result. Read alongside `obsessive-compulsive-disorder`, where that
threshold *was* derived empirically in 2025 — it can be done, and in Alzheimer's it has not been.

**Both sources are parties to the dispute, in opposite directions, and that turned out to be an
advantage.** Espay, Kepp and Herrup are prominent critics; **Selkoe originated the amyloid cascade
hypothesis** and Haass is a leading proponent. The page names both positions in the running text
(run plan §19.5) and then extracts **what both sides concede**: that the field has **no validated
definition of clinical meaningfulness**, that the aducanumab approval rested on a **post-hoc**
reanalysis even its defenders describe as post-hoc, and that the trials **may not be measuring the
toxic species**, since the proponents' own mechanism implicates soluble oligomers, which are
**invisible to amyloid PET**. **Where two partisan sources exist, take both and mine the overlap.**

**Five findings from the rest of the chapter that are teachable in their own right:**

- **Delirium prevention works; delirium treatment does not.** Multicomponent programmes (HELP and
  relatives) cut incidence — **RR 0.71** after hip fracture, **RR 0.42** in high-risk medical patients
  when family-delivered — but once delirium has started, *"the available evidence does not support the
  efficacy"* of the same interventions. **No benefit at all in low-risk patients**, and no effect on
  falls, length of stay or mortality.
- **The same drug, three answers.** Donepezil helps after **TBI**, is contraindicated in **mild
  neurocognitive disorder** (one guideline recommends deprescribing it), and is useless or harmful in
  **frontotemporal dementia**, where the cholinergic system is relatively preserved and a case series
  found **increased disinhibition in 4 of 12** treated patients. That is the argument for subtyping
  neurocognitive disorders, in the only currency that matters.
- **Two dementias where the standard response to agitation is the dangerous one** — fatal antipsychotic
  sensitivity in **Lewy body** disease, **parkinsonism and tardive antecollis** in bvFTD.
- **A criteria change can record improved practice rather than new knowledge.** Severe antipsychotic
  sensitivity was **downgraded** in the DLB criteria *because prescribing fell*, making the reaction
  too rare to be diagnostically useful.
- **Oral thiamine is not a weaker treatment for Wernicke encephalopathy; it is not a treatment.**
  Requiring the classic triad finds **23%** of cases against **85%** using Caine's two-of-four
  criteria — and Wernicke delirium is routinely mislabelled as alcohol withdrawal delirium, which the
  course teaches on a neighbouring page.

**Two new pages.** `neurocognitive-disorder-with-lewy-bodies` — the third major dementia, routinely
misdiagnosed as Alzheimer's, with **up to half of research-diagnosed Alzheimer cases showing
unsuspected Lewy pathology at autopsy**. And `substance-medication-induced-neurocognitive-disorder`,
which carries the chapter's only good news: alcohol-related impairment is **partially reversible**,
improving over a year or more of abstinence with increased brain volume.

**Two pages state what their source does not have** rather than writing around it —
`vascular-neurocognitive-disorder` records that its prevention framework rests on **no randomised
trials**, and the substance page opens with a **scope note** that the DSM category covers inhalants,
sedatives and medications while the evidence is almost entirely about alcohol.

Live state: **250 pages with bodies**, 1,343 wikilinks, 11 red links all to real catalogue slugs, 0
duplicate headings, queue clear, 127 ingest jobs, **0 published**. Gaps: `contested` 20,
`treatment` 18, `etiology` 15, `epidemiology` 8.

### Prevalence: an invariant, a concept page, and the first frontmatter field the reader shows (2026-08-03)

**Every `type='disorder'` page now carries exactly one `prevalence:` line in frontmatter — 108 of
108.** The starting state was worse than it looked: 63 pages had a value, 12 had a placeholder, and
**33 had no such field at all** — and a reader could not have told, because `WikiPage.jsx` rendered
none of them.

**"No figure in this source" is a value, not a gap.** 21 of the 108 say so explicitly, and the
distinction is the point:

- **Blank** means nobody looked.
- `factitious-disorder` — *"largely unknown — deception is intrinsic to the disorder and clinicians
  rarely record the diagnosis even in recognised cases (APA, 2022)"* — means somebody looked, and the
  absence has a cause worth teaching.
- `pedophilic-disorder` — stigma keeps people out of clinical samples, so published figures are
  unrepresentative **by construction**.
- `voyeuristic-disorder` — the source states 12% of males and 4% of females and, in the same passage,
  that the rate *is not known*. The field records that the numbers already on the page **must not be
  quoted**.

The reader shows these alongside the real rates. Hiding them would leave only the disorders that
happen to have been counted, which is the exact distortion the new concept page argues against.

**Values are derived, not researched.** Each was written from that page's own Epidemiology section,
which is already provenanced — so no new claim enters the corpus, and the frontmatter cannot drift
from the body's sources. That is why it ran as a plain `UPDATE` on `wiki_pages.content` rather than
through an ingest job: it is a restatement. The five triggers on `wiki_pages` handle the
bookkeeping — snapshot to a version, re-derive `needs`, re-derive the link graph, bump the
timestamp — and **wikilink count was unchanged at 1,286** across the 45-page edit, which is the check
that frontmatter-only edits touched no bodies.

**New `prevalence` concept page**, deliberately *not* a duplicate of `epidemiology` (which keeps
point/period/lifetime, incidence and comorbidity). It carries the finding the §19 campaign kept
producing from different chapters: **a published rate is a property of four decisions, none of which
is the disorder** — which manual defined a case, which instrument measured it, where the threshold sat,
and which sample was asked.

| Demonstration | Figure |
|---|---|
| **The manual decides the number** ([[delirium]]) | the same **200 patients** are **16%** delirious under ICD-10 and **28%** under DSM-III-R; ICD-10's sensitivity is **53.1%** |
| **A stable rate can hide an unstable category** ([[agoraphobia]]) | prevalence essentially unchanged DSM-IV → DSM-5, while **57.1% met both, 18.8% DSM-IV only, 24.2% DSM-5 only** |
| **The instrument and its threshold** ([[illness-anxiety-disorder]]) | **41 measures**, most with no validated cut-off; **4.3%–86%** across 58 cancer studies — and **28%–70%** holding instrument *and* cut-off constant |

Built as **three sequential versions under three ingest jobs** (run plan §19.3), so all three sources
appear under *Built from*. Figures borrowed from elsewhere — PTSD's 42% concordance, the arbitrary
Y-BOCS 16, gaming disorder's 30+ instruments — are cited inline and wikilinked to the pages where they
are fully provenanced.

**The label is the link.** `WikiPage.jsx` renders the value in a bordered line under the summary, with
the word **Prevalence** linking to the concept page. That gives **all 108 disorder pages a route there
without editing 108 bodies**. The alternative — a `[[prevalence]]` wikilink in every disorder page —
would have added ~108 graph edges carrying no analytical information and rewritten every page's version
history to do it. The concept page keeps **one** real backlink, from `epidemiology`, where the link is
in the body and is a genuine edge.
