duplicate headings, queue clear, 117 ingest jobs, **0 published**.

### The contested campaign completes Tier A (2026-08-02)

**`contested` empty: 47 → 21. Tier A pages with an empty `contested` section: 0.** Twenty-four pages
closed from twenty open-access journal sources in one session, using the strategy §29a's previous entry
set out — journals rather than textbooks, because critique is a different genre from description.

| Page | Source | Sections closed |
|---|---|---|
| `functional-neurological-symptom-disorder` | Stone et al. 2024, *World Psychiatry* | etiology, contested |
| `insomnia-disorder` | Krystal, Prather & Ashbrook 2019 | contested |
| `prolonged-grief-disorder` | Prigerson & Maciejewski 2024; Reed et al. 2022 | etiology, treatment, contested |
| `internet-gaming-disorder` | Reed et al. 2022 | contested |
| `generalized-anxiety-disorder`, `panic-disorder` | Gray et al. 2024 (WHO) | contested |
| `disruptive-mood-dysregulation-disorder` | Leibenluft 2017 | diagnosis, epidemiology, etiology, treatment, contested |
| `stimulant-use-disorder` | Newcorn 2025 | contested |
| `separation-anxiety-disorder` | Silove, Manicavasagar & Pini 2016 | contested |
| `obsessive-compulsive-disorder` | Cervin et al. 2022 + 2025 | contested |
| `neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-alzheimers-disease`, `vascular-neurocognitive-disorder` | Ravona-Springer et al. 2003 | contested |
| `binge-eating-disorder` | Amianto et al. 2015, *BMC Psychiatry* | contested |
| `adjustment-disorders` | Zapata-Ospina et al. 2023, *Front Psychiatry* | treatment, contested |
| `delirium` | Sepulveda et al. 2016, *BMC Psychiatry* | contested |
| `delusional-disorder` | González-Rodríguez & Seeman 2022 | etiology, treatment, contested |
| `narcolepsy` | Quaedackers, Pillen & Overeem 2021 | epidemiology, contested |
| `illness-anxiety-disorder` | Lebel et al. 2020, *PLOS ONE* | contested |
| `dissociative-amnesia` | Taïb et al. 2023, *Front Psychiatry* | contested |
| `dissociative-identity-disorder` | Brand et al. 2016, *Harvard Rev Psychiatry* | contested |
| `substance-withdrawal` | Jesse et al. 2017, *Acta Neurol Scand* | epidemiology, etiology, contested |
| `agoraphobia` | Roest et al. 2019, *Depress Anxiety* | contested |
| `erectile-disorder` | Dewitte et al. 2021 (ESSM) | contested |
| `specific-phobia` | Thng et al. 2020, *F1000Research* | contested |

**The search method is the reusable part.** The previous entry noted the campaign is *per page*, which
made it look expensive. Batching the **Europe PMC REST API** over a topic list fixes that: one shell
loop over 15-20 topics, printing `pmcid | year | journal | title`, produces a shortlist in a single
pass. Only shortlisted candidates get fetched — and **the verification fetch before writing stayed
mandatory**, because a search result gives a title, not a citation and not a licence.

**World Psychiatry alone does not cover this course.** Seventeen topics against it returned nothing for
phobia, dissociation, delirium, Alzheimer's, narcolepsy, adjustment disorder, PMDD, schizoaffective or
delusional disorder. Widening the journal set closed almost all of them. **Search the topic, not the
journal** — the earlier assumption that one flagship journal would carry the campaign was wrong.

**Prevalence is a property of the manual, and this round produced the clearest demonstration yet.**
Sepulveda et al. assessed **200 consecutive patients** against four criteria sets simultaneously:

| Criteria | Delirium prevalence | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| DSM-III-R | 28.0% | 81.6% |
| DSM-5 | 27.0% | 73.5% |
| DSM-IV | 21.0% | 71.4% |
| ICD-10 | **16.0%** | **53.1%** |

**ICD-10 misses nearly half of cases** in a condition where a missed case is an untreated medical
emergency. Agoraphobia gives the same lesson in the opposite form: prevalence is essentially
**unchanged** between DSM-IV and DSM-5 (1.4% → 1.5% lifetime) while **43% of cases are recognised by
one manual and not the other** — an unchanged rate concealing a substantially changed population.

**Reliability and accuracy trade off against each other, repeatedly.** DSM-5's delirium criteria have
the best inter-rater reliability of the four systems and slightly lower accuracy; *disorganised
thinking* was dropped after DSM-III-R **specifically to improve agreement among non-psychiatrists**,
and performed well phenomenologically when tested. DSM-5 collapsed primary and secondary insomnia into
one category because **the mechanism of insomnia is poorly understood** and clinicians could not tell
them apart — a nosological decision driven by the limits of raters, not by a finding about the
condition.

**Thresholds that decide who gets treated are often arbitrary.** The Y-BOCS score of **16** used as the
entry criterion for most OCD treatment trials has **no basis in empirical evidence** — so every efficacy
figure in that literature was produced in samples assembled by an arbitrary number. The empirically
derived "severe" threshold of 30 has positive predictive value of **43-49%**, which led its own authors
to state that **rationing access to intensive specialist treatment on the basis of it should be
questioned**.

**Three pages needed their denominator stated before their findings.** `adjustment-disorders` carries a
seven-row table distinguishing adjustment disorder from a depressive episode — from a **qualitative
study of four people**, and the page says so in bold immediately after the table, calling it a
hypothesis rather than a discriminant. `dissociative-amnesia` gives its imaging findings only after
stating the base: **22 studies, 49 patients, one prospective controlled study, mean quality 4.9/10**.
`specific-phobia` reports the largest effect sizes in the corpus alongside the fact that **3 of 33
studies used clinical samples** — in a disorder whose defining clinical feature is that people avoid
the treatment.

**Sources that are parties to their own dispute are now a pattern.** Brand et al. on DID are advocates
of the trauma model and authors of the guidelines their paper defends; the ESSM statement on erectile
dysfunction argues for the approach the society represents. Both join Volkow on addiction under the
same rule: **name the authorship position in the page text, then use the source's own numbers.**

**Licences varied per article, not per journal.** Gray et al. is **CC BY 4.0** — © World Health
Organization, licensed by the authors — inside a journal whose other content is not. Four sources are
**CC BY-NC-ND**, so cite-and-paraphrase only, no remixing. Two are CC BY-NC. Each was checked on the
retrieved record, not inferred.

**What remains: 21 `contested` gaps** — 19 Tier B, plus `substance-intoxication` and
`sleep-wake-disorders`. The Tier B remainder is harder: several have thin open-access review
literature and need a targeted search per page rather than another batch sweep.

Live state: **247 pages with bodies**, 1,286 wikilinks, 11 red links all resolving to real catalogue
slugs, 0 blue links to an empty page, 0 duplicate headings, queue clear, 114 ingest jobs, **0
published**.

### The contested campaign opens: World Psychiatry, and a change of source strategy (2026-08-02)

**The gap query changed the plan.** Asking what the corpus still declares missing, rather than what the next source might offer, showed that **`contested` is now the largest hole — 47 pages, 38% of all empty sections**, 22 of them Tier A. `treatment` follows at 27, `etiology` at 19, `epidemiology` at 11.

**More textbooks will not close it.** Five textbooks in, every one supplied presentation, prevalence, etiology and treatment — and every one left `contested` empty on most pages. Critique is a different genre, and the corpus already has the right vehicle for it: the **`debate` page type** and the **journal-article ingest** used for Fonagy, Shedler and Menchón.

**Proof of concept: PTSD**, from **Bryant, R. A. (2019), *Post-traumatic stress disorder: a state-of-the-art review of evidence and challenges*, World Psychiatry 18(3):259-269**, retrieved and verified on PMC. It closed the gap completely and produced the best `contested` section in the corpus:

- **Only 42% of trauma survivors are diagnosed with PTSD under *both* DSM-5 and ICD-11.** Two manuals, the same people, agreement on fewer than half the cases — which reframes every prevalence figure on the page, including the Canadian ones, as partly a property of the manual that produced it.
- **636,120 permutations** of how DSM-5 PTSD may present. Two people can carry the diagnosis with almost no symptoms in common, which is Bryant's explanation for why biomarkers have not been found.
- **The breadth/specificity trade-off costs something on both sides.** DSM-5 reaches more survivors; but moving beyond fear symptoms **undermines the evidence base of the exposure-based treatments the page recommends**.
- **Complex PTSD survives its validity test** — latent class analyses distinguish it from PTSD and from [[borderline-personality-disorder]], which was the main objection to admitting it. ICD-11 includes it; DSM-5 does not.
- **Only two-thirds of patients respond adequately to trauma-focused CBT**, which Bryant reads as evidence the definition is not capturing the essential mechanisms — **a failure of the category presenting as a failure of treatment**.

**Licence handled conservatively.** The PMC record shows "© 2019 World Psychiatric Association" with no explicit Creative Commons statement in the retrieved metadata, so it is treated as **free-to-read but not remixable** — cite and paraphrase, no extended verbatim reproduction. Same handling as StatPearls and the NAP gambling source, recorded in `licence_note` on the job. Much of World Psychiatry is CC-licensed; the conservative default costs nothing and can be relaxed once verified.

**The campaign is per-page, not per-source, and that is the planning point.** A textbook sweep covers a chapter at a time; this covers one page at a time. Each target needs a search, a **verification fetch**, a read and a write — and searches for OCD, bipolar, panic and GAD returned mostly *non*-World-Psychiatry work, so coverage has to be checked per disorder rather than assumed.

**Never write a citation from a search-result summary.** Two of the first candidates show why: `PMC11733476` looked like Brewin's 2025 PTSD review and is in fact **Maercker's commentary on it**, and the Wiley copy of Brewin **403s** to automated fetch. Both were caught by fetching before writing. **A fabricated citation in a reference corpus is worse than an empty section**, and PMC — not the publisher site — is the reliable route for this journal.

**Next targets**, all Tier A with empty `contested`: `obsessive-compulsive-disorder`, `bipolar-i-disorder`, `generalized-anxiety-disorder`, `panic-disorder`, `substance-use-disorder`, `dissociative-identity-disorder`, `neurocognitive-disorder-due-to-alzheimers-disease`, `delirium`, `binge-eating-disorder`. Where World Psychiatry has no matching review, **F1000Research** (already used for gambling), **BMC Psychiatry** and **Frontiers in Psychiatry** carry the same genre.

### The first student-facing page, and a standing verification obligation (2026-08-02)

**`student-support-resources`** — from **Kulzhabayeva, D. (2026), *Mental Health and Student Support Resources*, RADlab, University of Toronto**. Internal lab material compiled **2026-07-20**, not an openly licensed publication, used with the lab's own authority for the lab's own course.

**This closes the highest-priority safety gap in the corpus.** `suicide-and-self-harm` previously carried **only the US 988 line**, flagged as the one line on the page a student in distress might actually act on. It now carries the Canadian equivalents: the **9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline** (call or text 988, free and confidential anywhere in Canada, 24 hours), **Good2Talk** (1-866-925-5454, or text GOOD2TALKON to 686868, for Ontario post-secondary students), **U of T TELUS Health Student Support** (1-844-451-9700, 24 hours, all U of T students), the **St. George, UTM and UTSC** health and wellness centres — with same-day mental-health appointment routing for St. George — and **Find-A-Helpline** for students outside Canada.

One detail worth carrying into the literature: **Canada and the US share the 988 digits**, so a paper citing "988" may mean either service. Both pages say so.

**Two editorial decisions.**

The source document ends with a **study-specific research contact** — investigator name and email — because it was written to appear at the end of a *different* study's surveys. That was **omitted deliberately**: directing PSY240 students to another study's investigator would misdirect them. The omission is recorded in the ingest job's `result_json.omitted_deliberately`, so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight if anyone compares the page against the source.

And the page **states why it exists using the course's own findings** rather than as boilerplate. About **60% of people with suicidal thoughts do not seek help**, citing **low perceived need** and **wanting to deal with the problem alone** — not that treatment was unavailable. Only about **10% of people with gambling disorder ever seek treatment**. Fear of the stigma attached to a psychiatric diagnosis recurs as a barrier across the corpus. **The barrier the literature identifies is knowledge and reluctance, not scarcity** — which is precisely what a visible, specific list addresses. That makes the resource page an application of the content, not an attachment to it.

**It introduces an obligation the corpus did not previously have.** Every other page can go stale harmlessly; this one cannot. Phone numbers, URLs and hours change, so it carries three things: a visible ⚠ block on the page, a `staleness_warning` on the ingest job, and a **`verify_before_publishing: true` frontmatter flag** so a future publication pass can locate it **by query rather than by memory**. The instruction is explicit — re-verify every entry before students are given access and again each term, and **if a number cannot be verified, remove it rather than publish it unchecked**.

**One thing left open deliberately.** The page has a single inbound link, from `suicide-and-self-harm`, which is itself linked from eleven disorder pages — so it is one hop from most of the sensitive material. **One hop is a real barrier for a reader in distress**, but deciding where trigger-adjacent signposting belongs across a course is a pedagogical judgement for the instructor rather than a corpus-mechanics one. Run plan §17.4 records the bounded rule if it is wanted: link it from every page on which the corpus itself reports elevated suicide risk, which is currently eleven pages.

### The sweep completes: gap-first beats source-first (2026-08-02)

**Every section of all five sources is now in.** The remaining Cummings sections (1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 2.1, 2.4, 4.2, 5.1, 7.1) and the relevant Davies chapters produced **one new page and nine gap-closing updates**.

**The ordering principle is the transferable finding.** Instead of reading each section and asking what it offered, the declared `needs` and `annotations` lists were queried first, and only the sections that could close them were read. **Nine of the ten items closed a specific declared gap**, and all ten pages now carry **zero empty sections** — corpus empty sections fell **129 → 123** even though four new pages were added in the same period. Sweeping a source section by section produces bulk; sweeping it against a gap list produces closure.

| Page | Was | Closed by |
|---|---|---|
| **`psychopharmacology`** *(new)* | did not exist | Cummings 2.4 (Barron) |
| `deinstitutionalization` | `outcomes-and-criticisms` empty | Cummings 2.1 |
| `historical-traditions` | two sections empty | Cummings 2.1 |
| `mental-status-examination` | `limitations` annotated | Cummings 1.3 |
| `clinical-assessment` | `cultural-and-contextual-considerations` annotated | Cummings 1.2 |
| `medicalization-of-distress` | no Szasz at all | Cummings 1.2 |
| `body-dysmorphic-disorder` | `contested` empty | Cummings 4.2 |
| `schizophrenia` | `contested` empty | Davies ch 25–31 |
| `antipsychotic-medications` | `what-they-do-not-do` annotated | Davies ch 25–31 |
| `adhd` | MTA trial declared missing since Module 16 | Cummings 7.1 |

**The MTA trial closed the longest-standing declared gap in the corpus.** Four arms — community care, intensive behavioural treatment, stimulant medication, and the combination. **On core symptoms, medication was most effective and combined treatment was no better.** But behavioural treatment produced **less disruption at school**, allowed **lower stimulant doses** (which are better tolerated), and **higher parent satisfaction**. The trial that appears to show medication winning is the same trial establishing why behavioural treatment belongs in the package — a clean case of why one headline result is not a treatment recommendation.

**The ADHD parenting myth is refuted by an unusually clean design.** Cunningham and Barkley (1979) found mothers of children with ADHD less attentive and more controlling than mothers of typically developing children — then showed that **when the children were given stimulants, the mothers' parenting improved to match**. The causal arrow runs child → parent. Pelham et al. (1997) add that **a brief interaction with an impulsive child raised parents' alcohol consumption**. This is the corpus's best worked example of a reciprocal effect being mistaken for a unidirectional cause, and it reconciles "weak evidence for psychosocial *causes*" with "parent training *works*".

**Moral treatment and deinstitutionalisation failed the same way, a century apart.** Moral treatment was **"a victim of its own success"**: it worked best at **200 patients or fewer**, post-Civil-War immigration pushed US facilities to **1,000 or more**, staffing and funding collapsed — and **immigrants were denied the moral treatment given to native-born citizens even where the resources existed**. Teaching both collapses together shows the recurring failure is **resourcing and equity, not the humane principle**, which is the argument that matters when deinstitutionalisation is taught as a cautionary tale.

**The institutional model arrived in Canada as imperial policy.** Tuke's work produced the **County Asylums Act 1845**, extended to English colonies **including Canada, India, Australia and the West Indies** after maltreatment at a Kingston, Jamaica facility prompted a colonial audit; Dorothea Dix's work also reached Canada. That **partially** closes `non-western-and-global-histories` — partially, and the page says so, with Indigenous understandings of distress and the mental-health consequences of residential schools named as a gap a Canadian course cannot leave open.

**Szasz is now on the record properly**, with the argument's decisive vindication: he was **perhaps the first psychiatrist to openly challenge homosexuality as a diagnosis**, a case where the diagnosis genuinely was social disapproval in clinical dress. The page holds that against [[gender-dysphoria]], where the same argument is live and where removing the diagnosis would also remove access to funded care. **The critique was right once; that does not make it automatically right again**, and the corpus should treat it as neither settled objection nor settled refutation.

**The new `psychopharmacology` page** supplies what the medication pages lacked: ADME; **route of administration predicting abuse liability** — fast to the brain plus reward circuit equals high risk, and the *cues* become addictive too, which is why a smoker cannot avoid the trigger the way someone can avoid old haunts; cytochrome P450, enzyme induction and the **grapefruit-juice interaction** (85 drugs, including carbamazepine, diazepam and fluvoxamine); the **four metaboliser categories**, where the ultra-extensive metaboliser never gets benefit and the poor metaboliser gets side effects, and **both look like treatment failure while neither is**; and the two populations **excluded from the trials that licensed their drugs** — children, where only ADHD stimulants are well established, and older adults, projected to consume **40% of prescriptions by 2030** while being routinely excluded from trials for having comorbidities.

**Two sections were read and produced nothing, which is worth recording.** Cummings 5.1 and 7.1 contain **no substantive Canadian prose** — an earlier keyword count suggested otherwise because it was matching **reference-list entries** (Canadian Journal of Psychiatry, Schizophrenia Society of Canada, CADDAC). 7.1 was swept anyway for the MTA trial and stimulant-diversion material; 5.1 added nothing beyond Davies. **Count keyword hits in the body, not the references** — a citation to a Canadian journal is not Canadian content, and the earlier scan overstated Canadian coverage on that basis.

**And the pre-accept checks caught two more real errors.** Appended content had **re-created two headings as duplicates** rather than filling the existing empty sections, and a `clinical-assessment` block had landed **after `## Contested`** instead of inside its own section. Both repaired before acceptance. That is **three consecutive runs** in which these checks caught a genuine structural error — they are not ceremony.

### The skeleton completes: suicide and self-harm (2026-08-02)

**Tier A 54/54. Foundations 14/14. Overviews 16/16.** Every page the catalogue marks as central, foundational or structural now has a body. **Only Tier B remains incomplete, at 33/46.**

`suicide-and-self-harm` was the last, and had been the most-linked red link in the corpus at **11 inbound references** — accumulated across eleven disorder pages that each reported suicide risk with nowhere to point. Written from **Davies (2025) chapter 22**, adapted from Coursehero under CC BY-SA.

**Safe messaging was applied, and it cost the page nothing.** The source includes a named-individual case study with circumstantial detail. The page **omits the circumstances and method entirely** and keeps only the general point — that risk is often invisible to those closest to the person, so **absence of visible warning signs is not evidence of absence of risk**. Means-restriction evidence (higher rates in households with firearms) **is** retained, because that is protective public-health content rather than method information, and that distinction is the one to apply next time a source mixes clinical material with case narrative. An `editorial_note` on the ingest job records the decision so it is not silently reversed later. The page also opens with a short reader-facing note pointing to the crisis-line section.

**The ideation gap is the organising finding.** Roughly **10.6 million US adults experience serious suicidal thoughts**, against **1.4 million attempts** and **47,000 deaths**. Jobes and Joiner's (2019) argument is that prevention research, clinical treatment and national health policy are organised around the two smaller numbers — so a field that measures what it can count systematically under-serves the largest affected group. Berman's (2009) three-part model (vulnerability *plus* means *plus* absent protective factors) is what makes the 90%-have-a-diagnosis figure readable in both directions, and each leg is separately modifiable, which is how the prevention section is built.

**The treatment evidence is the strongest in the corpus, and unusually it comes with magnitudes:**

| Intervention | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Crisis Response Plan** | attempts reduced **76%** at 6 months vs no-harm contracts |
| **Brief CBT** (12 sessions) | **60% less likely** to attempt at 24 months |
| **Cognitive Therapy for Suicide Prevention** | **50% less likely** to attempt at 18 months |
| **Caring contacts** (Motto & Bostrom) | a letter every 4 months for 5 years **reduced suicides** |
| **CAMS** | reduces ideation and distress, increases hope and retention; **as good as DBT** on attempts |
| **DBT** | reduces attempts and self-harm; **ideation results inconsistent across RCTs** |

**The pattern is the teachable part: treatments that target suicidality *directly* outperform treating an underlying disorder and expecting the risk to follow.** That runs against how the rest of this course handles comorbidity, and it is why these interventions exist as a category.

**A clean displaced-practice case sits alongside it.** Coercive **no-harm contracts** — asking a patient to promise *not* to act — have been replaced by **stabilization planning**, which plans what the person *will* do in a crisis, and which is now standard across US Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense. See [[treatments-that-harm]] and [[evidence-based-practice]]. **Caring contacts** deserve separate note as among the lowest-cost interventions anywhere in this course with a demonstrated mortality effect.

**And the barrier that limits all of it: about 60% of people with suicidal thoughts do not seek help** — citing **low perceived need** and **wanting to deal with the problem alone**, not unavailability of treatment.

**Two gaps are flagged on the page, and one is urgent.** **Non-suicidal self-injury** is in the page's own title and absent from the source entirely. And **the crisis line given is US-only (988)** — the page flags that the **Canadian 9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline** and provincial services must be stated, **with number and hours verified before publishing**. That is the single highest-priority verification item outstanding in the corpus, because it is the one line on the page a student in distress might actually act on. Canadian rates generally, and rates among First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities in particular, cannot be substituted from a US source.

### Tier A completes: gambling disorder, and two licences on one page (2026-08-02)

**Tier A 53 → 54/54.** Every Tier A page in the catalogue now has a body. `gambling-disorder` was the last, and the one no textbook in this corpus covered at all — the WSU substance module mentions it zero times, and neither the Canadian text nor Davies has a chapter for it.

**Two sources, and only one is remixable.** This is the first page here built from sources with materially different licences, and the handling matters:

| Source | Licence | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Menchón et al. (2018)**, F1000Research 7:434 | **CC BY 4.0** — fully remixable | Current clinical picture: treatment, pharmacology, risk factors, subgroups |
| **National Research Council (1999)**, *Pathological Gambling: A Critical Review*, National Academies Press | **Not openly licensed** — copyrighted, freely readable on NCBI Bookshelf | DSM-III/III-R/IV criteria history, **summarised not reproduced** |

The NAP source is handled the way the run plan prescribes for StatPearls: **read, cite, paraphrase, do not remix**. No criteria list was reproduced verbatim; the page describes the *evolution* of the classification instead — which is both the licence-safe route and the better teaching content. A `licence_note` field on each ingest job records which terms apply, so the distinction survives independently of the page text.

**The reclassification is the spine of the page.** DSM-5 moved gambling disorder into *Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders* — **the first behavioural addiction placed alongside the substance disorders** — on the basis of shared criteria, symptomatology, genetic vulnerability, comorbidity, biomarkers and cognitive deficits. From **DSM-III (1980) through DSM-IV (1994)** the same behaviour sat under *Impulse Control Disorders Not Elsewhere Classified*, framed as a failure to resist impulses and described through indebtedness, family disruption and non-violent financial crime. Teaching both framings together shows a diagnostic category being **re-theorised rather than discovered**.

Menchón et al. add the point that makes this more than filing: the reclassification **changes the perceived dangerousness of the disorder, and attitudes about the chances of recovery and about responsibility for creating and solving gambling problems.** A classification decision doing moral work, not only taxonomic work.

**Three numbers carry the page.**

- **Only about 10% of people with gambling disorder ever seek treatment**, and treatment-seeking rises with severity. That single figure reframes everything else: the clinical literature describes a tenth of the affected population, selected for severity. Named barriers are lack of knowledge about options and **fear of the stigma attached to a psychiatric diagnosis** — so the reclassification that made gambling a recognised disorder may also have raised the barrier to seeking help for it.
- **32% of treatment-seeking patients had experienced suicidal ideation and 17% had attempted suicide at least once**; another study found **30.2% reporting an attempt in the 12 months before treatment**.
- **No drug is approved for gambling disorder anywhere.** Opioid antagonists (naltrexone, nalmefene) are the best-supported class, and the meta-analytic verdict is **"a small but significant benefit"** over placebo. Only 2 of 5 SSRI trials beat placebo; bupropion did not; N-acetylcysteine is positive in a pilot only. Most studies are open trials with small samples and scarce follow-up.

Two further items worth keeping: the risk-factor meta-analysis is **unusually well specified** — 13 individual, 1 relationship and 1 community risk factor, plus **three protective factors**, which is rare in this corpus — and **three replicated subgroups** (behaviourally conditioned, emotionally vulnerable, antisocial impulsive) support treatment matching rather than one protocol for all.

**The Canadian gap here is a conflict of interest, not merely missing data.** Every figure is US or European. In Canada **provincial governments both regulate gambling and depend on its revenue**, and provincial self-exclusion programmes have no equivalent in this literature. Neither source mentions industry funding of gambling research. Recorded as a declared gap.

**What remains.** `suicide-and-self-harm` is now the **single unwritten page across Tier A, foundations and overviews**, and at **11 inbound red links** it is the most-linked target in the corpus — gambling disorder alone added several. Davies (2025) chapter 22, *Suicide and Prevention*, is the source.

### The sixteen overviews close, and how to use a source you cannot trust everywhere (2026-08-02)

**Goerling, E., & Wolfe, E. (2022). *Introduction to Human Sexuality.* Open Oregon Educational Resources.** WXR export plus PDF; URL verified live. Book licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with per-chapter sub-licences — **ch 17 adapted from Miller's *Clinical Perspectives in Abnormal Psychology* under CC BY 4.0**, **ch 16 from Walinga & Stangor's *Introduction to Psychology – 1st Canadian Edition* (BCcampus)**. The WXR is dated 2022 while the live edition is now ©2024; the citation names 2022, the copy actually read, and the job records the discrepancy.

**13 pages. Tier A 49 → 53/54. Tier B 26 → 33/46. Overviews 14 → 16/16 — complete.** Lecture 7 Tier A is now 5 of 5. Only `gambling-disorder` and `suicide-and-self-harm` remain unwritten at Tier A and foundation, and both have identified sources.

**The taxonomy had flagged the paraphilic overview for rewrite-level review** — *"lecture-hall-provocative framing… must not be laundered into a reference page."* Chapter 16 justified the flag, and how that was handled is the part worth keeping.

**Four passages were treated as source defects and named on the page**, rather than reproduced or quietly removed:

1. A **cultural-relativism passage** presenting adult–child sexual contact as normal in some societies. The pages say plainly this is not teachable as cultural variation: the issue is **capacity to consent**, and the passage confuses a descriptive claim about practices with a normative one about harm.
2. A **relayed conflation of pedophilia with homosexuality**, which the source reproduces without rebuttal. The page states it is **false** and spells out the distinction.
3. **"Women who wear low-cut gowns are exhibitionists in a sense"** — not a DSM criterion, no diagnostic content, and it imports victim-blaming into a chapter about non-consensual acts.
4. **A voyeurism prevalence that contradicts itself** — 12% of males and 4% of females stated, then "the prevalence rate of this abnormality is not known" in the same passage. The page says do not quote it.

**The general rule: when a source contains material that should not be taught, name it as a defect on the page.** Dropping it silently leaves the next person to rediscover it from the source; reproducing it launders it. A `source_quality_warning` field now carries the same caution at the job level, so the warning survives independently of the pages.

**What the chapter gets right is the distinction the category depends on.** A **paraphilia** is an unusual sexual interest requiring no treatment; a **paraphilic disorder** is one that distresses the person *or* victimises others (Lehmiller, 2019). **Consent is the organising axis**, and it sorts the eight disorders more usefully than the DSM's own ordering — four are non-consensual by definition, three are potentially consensual and turn on distress. The strongest counter-pathologising evidence in the corpus also sits here: **BDSM practitioners show higher subjective wellbeing than average, less neuroticism, more openness and conscientiousness, and no correlation with childhood sexual assault** (Joyal, 2018).

**And the largest honest gap this run created:** the paraphilia chapter supplies **no etiology and no treatment for any of its disorders**. Both sections are empty across every paraphilic page. The chapter is descriptive and forensic, not clinical — and for `pedophilic-disorder` that omission is consequential, since the prevention literature on non-offending help-seekers is exactly what is missing.

**On the dysfunction side, the threshold is the teachable point.** Diagnosis requires six months, presence in **75% or more of sexual situations**, and clinically significant distress — while the headline figures everyone quotes (**43% of women, 31% of men**; Laumann et al., 1999) measure self-reported difficulty over twelve months and apply none of that. The gap between those two numbers is where the medicalisation argument about female sexual dysfunction lives, and a page carrying both without saying so would mislead.

Two further items worth keeping. **The DSM-5 merger of dyspareunia and vaginismus** into [[genito-pelvic-pain-penetration-disorder]] was done because the two could not be reliably distinguished — a candid case of a reliability problem solved by redefinition. And **[[transvestic-disorder]] asks the chapter's sharpest question in the source's own words**: why is cross-dressing pathologised in one direction and not the other, and should distress be evaluated as distress at the behaviour or distress at the culture's response to it? That generalises well past this diagnosis — a distress criterion that does not ask where the distress comes from will reliably find disorder in whoever a society treats worst.

**Five sources in, the keyword-scan-before-planning rule paid off in the opposite direction from last time.** It confirmed full coverage of both DSM chapters before any work began, and correctly predicted 13 pages.

| Source | Expected | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| *Behavioral Disorders of Childhood* | Module 16 etiology/treatment | as expected |
| Cummings, *Abnormal Psychology* | "Canadian content" | partial — 9 chapters |
| Davies, *Adult Psychopathology* | "sleep and sexual" | partial — sleep only |
| Goerling & Wolfe, *Human Sexuality* | "sex and gender content" | **as expected — both chapters closed** |

### Sleep and gender dysphoria, from a fourth source (2026-08-02)

**Davies, C. (2025). *Adult Psychopathology.* University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries.** PDF only — 565 pages, Pressbooks/Prince output with a clean text layer, so `pdftotext -layout` was sufficient and no image route was needed. The canonical URL was **verified live** at `openbooks.library.umass.edu/adultpsychopathology/`; the PDF carries no URL of its own, and the run plan's rule against citations without a source link meant checking rather than guessing.

**Three licences in one book.** The default is **CC BY-NC 4.0** — the first non-ShareAlike source in this corpus — but the chapters actually used carry their own: **23–24 (gender dysphoria) adapted from Coursehero under CC BY-SA**, **47–48 (sleep) adapted from OpenStax *Psychology 2e* under CC BY 4.0**. The citation names the chapter's licence, not the book's. **Check the per-chapter attribution line, not just the copyright page** — a compiled OER can carry three licences at once.

**Six pages. Tier A 46 → 49/54, overviews 13 → 14/16.**

**`gender-dysphoria`** is the one that mattered most. The taxonomy had flagged it for **rewrite-level review** — the lecture deck carries dated terminology alongside current material and "must not be laundered into a reference page". A 2025 source makes that tractable: the rename from *gender identity disorder* after criticism that the term was stigmatising, the DSM-5 move out of the sexual-disorders category into one of its own, the separation of the child diagnosis from the adult one, and the **post-transition specifier** with the reason it exists — so that people who have transitioned can continue to receive ongoing treatment rather than losing access by succeeding. The page is written *against* the terminology history rather than smoothing it over, and leads with the three distinctions that do the work: being transgender is not a disorder, gender nonconformity is not gender dysphoria, and the diagnosis names distress rather than identity. The **0.6% of US adults identifying as transgender against ~0.01% diagnosed** makes that last point quantitative.

**Its contested section is the sharpest case of a two-way trade-off in the course.** The diagnosis is criticised for placing the problem in the individual rather than in a society that disapproves — and it is also what makes many insurers cover gender-confirming care, without which those treatments could be classed as cosmetic rather than medically necessary. Removing the label would relieve the stigma at the cost of the access. Most [[medicalization-of-distress]] cases in this course run one way; this one does not, and that is what makes it worth teaching.

**Five sleep pages** — `insomnia-disorder`, `narcolepsy`, `obstructive-sleep-apnea-hypopnea`, `parasomnias`, and the `sleep-wake-disorders` overview. The overview leads with normal sleep architecture (REM/NREM, the circadian and homeostatic mechanisms, pons for REM and hypothalamus/thalamus for slow-wave) because most of these disorders are defined as disruptions of a specific part of it, and **30–50% of the population experiences a sleep disorder at some point** — the highest-prevalence chapter in the course.

Two findings worth keeping. **Sleepwalking**: benzodiazepines did not alleviate it, but *every* sleepwalking patient who also had a sleep-related breathing problem improved markedly once the breathing was treated (Guilleminault et al., 2005) — treat the apnea and the parasomnia may resolve, which argues some sleepwalking is secondary rather than primary. And **hypnotics for insomnia** are described as causing dependence, altering the sleep cycle and **increasing insomnia over time** — a treatment that worsens what it treats, which is exactly the [[treatments-that-harm]] pattern and the clearest pharmacological instance of it here.

**What it does not cover is now a three-source pattern.** No sexual dysfunctions, no paraphilic disorders, **no gambling** — verified by keyword scan across the full 910 KB extraction, not inferred from the contents page. The only sexual/paraphilic mentions are rows in the DSM chapter-list table.

| Source | Expected to fill | Actually covered |
|---|---|---|
| *Behavioral Disorders of Childhood* | Module 16's etiology/treatment | delivered — 17 of 18 pages |
| Cummings, *Abnormal Psychology* | "Canadian content" | 9 chapters; **no** sleep, sexual, substance, eating, dissociative, somatic, NCD |
| Davies, *Adult Psychopathology* | "sleep and sexual disorders" | **sleep yes, sexual no** |

**Establish coverage before planning work.** One keyword scan of the extracted text settles it; a table of contents does not, because a chapter can name a topic it merely lists.

**What is left is now one coherent block plus one straggler.** Five Tier A pages and two overviews reduce to **a single source covering DSM chapters 13 (sexual dysfunctions) and 19 (paraphilias)**, plus **NIMH for `gambling-disorder`**, which is a behavioural addiction no textbook here covers. The paraphilic overview also carries a rewrite-level review flag, for lecture-hall-provocative framing in the deck.

**And `suicide-and-self-harm` is writable for the first time** — Davies has a *Suicide and Prevention* chapter. It is the only unwritten foundation and the most-linked red link in the corpus, and it is the immediate next job.

### The Canadian text: a third source, and the numbers that reverse (2026-08-02)

**Cummings, J. A. (2020). *Abnormal Psychology.* University of Saskatchewan Open Press.** CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so remixable on the same terms as the WSU books. HTML export plus native PDF in `PSY240resources/`.

**Cite by section, with the section's own authors.** The book is compiled from OERs — a *different* Bridley & Daffin volume (*Essentials of Abnormal Psychology*, ed. Cuttler), OpenStax, and Noba — and **each section carries its own author list**: 2.4 is Susan Barron alone, 8.1 is Pelphrey and Campoli, 2.5 is Strauss and Cummings. A whole-book citation would misattribute most of it. The canonical URL is `openpress.usask.ca/abnormalpsychology/`, **not** the one in the book's own metadata sample citation, which has a typo. `scripts/wsu-module-extract.mjs` now matches section titles as well as `Module N`, since this book numbers sections `1.1`, `3.1`.

**Establish chapter coverage first.** This book has **no sleep-wake, sexual, paraphilic, substance, eating, dissociative, somatic or neurocognitive chapters** — so it does not close §4's uncovered Tier A list, and it does not unblock the three remaining overviews. A new source is not a general-purpose gap filler, and checking which chapters exist is the first move, not the last.

**Canadian prevalence is a correctness fix, and it does not run one way.** [[major-depressive-disorder]] lifetime is **11.2% in Canada against 16.6% in the US** — a US textbook overstates Canadian lifetime risk by roughly half. But [[generalized-anxiety-disorder]] is **8.7% lifetime in Canada against 5.7% in the US**, the opposite direction, while [[social-anxiety-disorder]] agrees closely across both (13% and 12.1%). So there is no rule of thumb to apply; each figure has to be looked up.

**Three findings have no US-source equivalent.**

- **Cluster B personality disorders in Quebec: 13 years of life expectancy lost for men, 9 for women** (Cailhol et al., 2017), from a whole-province administrative cohort. The DSM-derived material describes Cluster B in terms of interpersonal difficulty and treatment obstacles; this reframes it as carrying a physical-health and mortality profile, and gives the treatment discussion its stakes.
- **A third of Canadian adults have a panic attack in a given year; 1–2% are diagnosed with panic disorder.** The cleanest available demonstration that what defines [[panic-disorder]] is the persistent apprehension about further attacks, not the attack itself.
- **Sexual and gender minorities in Ontario: 67.7% lifetime depression among sexual minorities, 72% among gender liminal people, 66.4% current depression among FtM trans participants** (Williams et al., 2017; Rotondi et al., 2011, Trans PULSE). The largest disparities in the corpus, and from community rather than clinical samples — which matters, because the sampling-artefact explanation offered for other sex differences does not obviously apply.

Also Canadian and consequential: **76% of Canadians are trauma-exposed but only ~8% of those develop PTSD**; **Canadian Armed Forces lifetime PTSD 11.1%**; **OCD more common at lower incomes**, an association absent from the DSM material; and Ontario's 2019 autism funding changes, which had **families leaving the province to obtain services**. Where access is decided provincially, "does the treatment work" and "can you get it" stop being separable questions.

**Six pages the WSU books have no equivalent for.** [[evidence-based-practice]], defined by the **Canadian Psychological Association (2012)** and three-legged — best research evidence, critical evaluation of it, *and* client specificity, the last being what stops EBP collapsing into "use whatever has the best trial". [[empirically-supported-treatments]], with four substantive objections including the **manualisation selection effect** (therapies expressible as step-by-step rules were prioritised, which selects on form rather than efficacy) and payers **funding only listed approaches, which the source says was never the intent**. **[[treatments-that-harm]]** — Lilienfeld's potentially harmful therapies, which **closes the most-repeated `Needs research` line in the corpus**: every "what does not work" note now has a page to point at, and [[psychological-debriefing]], scared-straight, deviancy training and the discredited attachment therapies are collected there. [[eco-anxiety]]. And three therapy orientations the WSU books never describe — [[person-centered-therapy]], [[mindfulness-based-therapy]] and [[acceptance-and-commitment-therapy]] — the mindfulness page carrying one of the few explicit magnitude statements anywhere in this corpus (**moderate** improvement for anxiety and depression, Hofmann et al., 2010).

**Diathesis-stress is now stated formally.** `integrative-model` had declared that gap since Module 02, and the handoff had explicitly earmarked a new text to fix it. The Canadian book's *Biological Model* chapter names the framework, uses it to explain why one identical twin develops [[schizophrenia]] and the other does not, and — the part usually left out — adds **protective factors**: a consistent, loving, supportive upbringing modifies the response to stress. That is the frame in which the corpus's most striking unexplained findings (under 10% of severely neglected children developing [[reactive-attachment-disorder]], ~8% of trauma-exposed Canadians developing PTSD) become proper questions rather than curiosities. The page's second gap, **comparative effect sizes**, remains open.

**One check earned its keep.** The pre-accept duplicate-heading check caught a second `## Epidemiology` on [[social-anxiety-disorder]] before acceptance. Rewriting it as a subsection also surfaced a subtler problem: the incoming lifetime figures (13%, 12.1%) sat beside existing point-prevalence figures (~7% US, 0.5–2.0% worldwide) and would have read as self-contradictory. The page now says which window each rate refers to.

Nine of seventeen sections swept. Run plan §11.4 lists the eight remaining with expected targets — **2.4 Psychopharmacology** (pharmacokinetics, metabolism, the grapefruit-juice interaction, juveniles and the elderly) is the highest-value, since the corpus's medication pages are mechanism-only. **55 image markers across the book remain unread natively**; none was needed so far, but 2.3 and 2.4 are the sections most likely to carry content as figures.

Live state: **222 pages with bodies**, 1,050 wikilinks, 0 off-catalogue red links, 0 duplicate headings, queue clear, **0 published**.

### Ten chapter overviews, and what an overview is for (2026-08-02)

**Overviews 3/16 → 13/16.** Every one that could be written from ingested material now exists. The three that do not — `sleep-wake-disorders`, `paraphilic-disorders`, `sexual-dysfunctions` — are §4's uncovered list wearing a different hat: **all of their member pages are unwritten**, because the textbook has no chapter for sleep-wake or for any of Lecture 7. An overview whose members are all empty has no source at all, so those three wait for the incoming material. **Check member coverage before scheduling an overview** is the rule that came out of this.

Written: mood, psychosis and the schizophrenia spectrum, personality, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and related, somatic symptom and related, trauma- and stressor-related, dissociative, feeding and eating, substance-related and addictive. **7.4k–12.3k chars each, zero empty sections across all ten** — matching what the `neurocognitive-disorders` pilot predicted.

**Method: synthesise from the member pages, cite the module.** The members are already faithful renderings of their module and carry figures that have been checked, so building the map from them is *more* accurate than re-reading the chapter and re-deriving numbers — and the citation still traces to the module, because that is where the content originated. Each overview got its own `reference` job with `target_slug` set (`ingest_jobs_target_slug_ck` requires it when `source_type='reference'`).

**What an overview is for became clear only by writing ten of them.** The useful ones do something the member pages structurally cannot: put the chapter's numbers in one table, where the outliers become visible. That is where the teaching value concentrated every single time.

- **Personality disorders** — the DSM-5-TR Table 13.1 grid. Two disorders were found at **0.0%** by one national survey and at **6.2%** and **1.8%** by another. The three estimates do not merely differ; they disagree about whether the disorders are detectable. Best epidemiology teaching material in the corpus, and an argument about method rather than about people.
- **Feeding and eating** — anorexia and bulimia run roughly **10:1 female**, while **binge-eating disorder is close to even**. The disorder with the least body-image content has the most even sex ratio, which complicates the simple sociocultural account students usually arrive with.
- **Substance-related** — **~9% of US teens and adults against ~22% of Native Americans**, reported with no explanation whatsoever. Teaching that rate without its colonial, socioeconomic and health-access context teaches a stereotype. This is the single clearest place in the corpus where Canadian material is a *requirement*: the equivalent data concerns First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities inside a specific policy and treaty history and cannot be imported from a US source.
- **Dissociative** — **~50% of adults report a transient depersonalization episode in life** against a 1–2% disorder prevalence. The course's cleanest continuum-with-normality case.
- **Mood** — ~30% of relatives affected on the unipolar side against bipolar heritability estimates near **90%**.
- **OCD-related** — the reference disorder that supplies the chapter's name, etiology and treatment model (**OCD, ~1.2%**) is rarer than three of the four conditions grouped around it.

**They also surfaced a structural pattern no single page could show.** Four chapters develop their etiology on one member and extend it to the rest by assumption: psychosis (schizophrenia only), trauma (PTSD only), OCD-related (OCD only), somatic (class level only). Each overview now states this explicitly instead of implying a chapter-wide account that does not exist — the same rule recorded for trichotillomania and excoriation in the companion-volume entry: **when a source generalises across a category, name the member the evidence was actually collected on.**

**One wrong call, made and retracted the same day.** While gathering material, 168 markdown-style links (`[text](slug.md)`) across 35 pages looked like a systematic defect, and the claim was made that they never reached `wiki_links` and understated the graph by that many edges. **That was false.** `sync_wiki_links()` parses both link forms explicitly, and `src/academic/fieldguide/wiki/wikiText.js` normalises `[[…]]` *into* `[label](slug.md)` precisely so one renderer handles both syntaxes. The link total was unchanged at 802 across the edit — visible immediately, and the proof.

The conversion had already been applied before the claim was checked. It is harmless — display text is preserved exactly and the corpus now uses one syntax — but it wrote a false rationale into 35 version-history notes, which were corrected in place afterwards. **The lesson is ordering, and it is the one §9 already teaches about slugs:** the check that would have caught this was a single query against `sync_wiki_links()`, and running it first would have cost nothing. A corpus-wide "defect" that nobody has noticed is more likely a misreading of the schema than a real bug — verify the mechanism before mass-editing on the strength of it.

Live state: **214 pages with bodies**, 988 wikilinks, 19 red links all resolving to real catalogue slugs, 0 blue links to an empty page, 0 duplicate headings, 0 off-catalogue disorders, queue clear, 58 ingest jobs, **0 published**. ### The companion volume: closing a declared-scope gap (2026-08-02)

Module 16 left **36 empty Etiology and Treatment sections** across 18 pages, not by omission but because its authors said twice that those topics belonged to a different book. That book — **Bridley & Daffin, *Behavioral Disorders of Childhood*, 3rd ed. (2022)**, same authors, same series, same CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence, same section format — was ingested the same day and closed **34 of the 36**, across **17 of the 18 pages**. The exception is `communication-disorders`, which has no chapter in the companion either and stays gapped honestly.

Corpus effect: empty sections **142 → 108**, annotations **60 → 79**. That second number moving up is the point — material that was an instructor-sized hole is now present prose carrying a student-sized ask.

**Getting the source was the part that went wrong, and the lesson is procedural.** Pressbooks publishes this book only as `mpdf` and `wxr`; `?type=xhtml` returns 500. Rather than stopping to ask, the session built a workaround — scraping nine live chapter pages one at a time. Norm had both the PDF and the WXR export, put them in `PSY240resources/` as soon as he saw what was happening, and set a standing rule: **when a download fails in a way that would compromise the approach, stop and ask rather than routing around it.** The workaround was also simply worse. The WXR is one local file holding every chapter's HTML in `content:encoded` CDATA, so a run is reproducible and does not depend on the site being reachable. It was verified against the scrape on Module 11 — 34,277 characters against 33,764, the difference being the title line — before switching, and the scraper was then deleted rather than left around to be reused.

Tooling was consolidated at the same time: `scripts/lib/pressbooks-md.mjs` now holds the one HTML→markdown converter (including the `<img>` → `[[IMAGE: file]]` rule that keeps a dropped figure loud), used by both `wsu-module-extract.mjs` for the parent book's single-file XHTML export and `pressbooks-wxr-extract.mjs` for WXR books. Two source formats, one code path, so extractions cannot drift.

**Ten ingest jobs, not one.** Attribution is a licence condition, and the parent book established citing the specific module. Each of the nine source chapters therefore got its own job row and citation, plus a tenth **whole-book** row for `neurodevelopmental-disorders`, which synthesises Modules 7–10 and cannot honestly claim any single one. Verified after acceptance: `adhd` reports two sources — Module 10 of the companion and Module 16 of the parent — each correctly named. The whole-book citation initially rendered with a stray "In"; it was corrected **at the job**, and the page updated itself, which is exactly the property that makes `edit_page()` the wrong tool for new content.

**The pages were spliced, not retyped.** These landed as `action='replace'` versions built in SQL with `substr()`/`position()` around the `## Etiology` and `## Contested` anchors, with the frontmatter `sources:` entry spliced in at the `---` boundary. Anchor uniqueness and ordering were checked across all 18 pages *before* the first insert — exactly one `## Etiology`, one `## Contested`, correctly ordered, one frontmatter close. Only the new prose was written by hand, and 17 multi-thousand-character pages stayed byte-identical outside the two sections being filled. This is the "prefer splicing over retyping long bodies" lesson applied at scale: a missed anchor raises instead of silently writing something mangled.

**What the companion does not fix makes the Canadian requirement sharper, not softer.** Its treatment sections are **entirely US-institutional** — IEPs under IDEA, insurance-gated ABA (the book is blunt that insurers fund ABA only with an autism diagnosis, making a broadly applicable therapy autism-exclusive in practice), US state screening rates. So `intellectual-developmental-disorder`, `specific-learning-disorder`, `autism-spectrum-disorder` and the `neurodevelopmental-disorders` overview each now carry an explicit declared gap naming provincial frameworks, CADDRA, and the distinction between a school-board designation and a DSM diagnosis. The book also **names programmes and reports response rates without ever giving an effect size**, which is now the single most repeated `Needs research` line in the corpus. And `contested` remains empty on nine pages: the companion has no more critical apparatus than the parent.

One methodological note kept in the run plan: the companion's OCD-related etiology is written for OCD and then applied to trichotillomania and excoriation, while the same chapter states that environmental factors matter more for the other OCD-related disorders than for OCD itself. Both pages say so explicitly rather than inheriting the OCD account silently. **When a source generalises across a category, the page should say which member the evidence was actually collected on.**

### Module 16 closes the sweep: the third kind of gap, and why it is the good kind (2026-08-02)

**All sixteen modules are ingested.** Module 16 by direct parse produced **18 pages** — the six remaining Lecture 10 Tier A entries (`adhd`, `autism-spectrum-disorder`, `conduct-disorder`, `intellectual-developmental-disorder`, `oppositional-defiant-disorder`, `specific-learning-disorder`), nine Tier B spanning four other lectures, and **two overviews** (`neurodevelopmental-disorders` at 11.6k chars, `disruptive-impulse-control-and-conduct-disorders` at 9.4k). Tier A **40 → 46/54**, Tier B **14 → 24/46**, overviews **1 → 3/16**, and **Lecture 10 complete at 9 of 9**. Zero slug misses, zero duplicate headings, zero off-catalogue pages, review queue clear.

**The count is not the finding.** Module 16 states twice — once in its module overview and again in its recap — that it covers *clinical presentation, prevalence, comorbidity and differential diagnosis* **only**, referring readers to a companion volume for etiology, assessment and treatment. Every page built from it therefore has three real sections and **two genuinely empty ones: 36 etiology/treatment gaps that re-reading the source cannot close**.

That is a **third gap class**, and keeping the three apart matters because they are indistinguishable in a coverage count and have different remedies:

| Class | Example | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Not in the source at all | `gambling-disorder` — zero mentions in Module 11 | A different source |
| Present but carved differently | alcohol / cannabis / opioid / stimulant, distributed across Module 11's drug-class partition | Reference mode against the same source |
| **Out of the source's declared scope** | Module 16's etiology and treatment | **The companion volume that holds it** |

The third is the good kind: it names its own fix. **Bridley & Daffin, *Behavioral Disorders of Childhood*** (https://opentext.wsu.edu/behavioral-disorders-childhood/) is the same authors, same series, same CC BY-NC-SA licence and same section format, written to cover precisely what Module 16 withholds for precisely these disorders. One ingest closes the largest single block of gaps in the corpus, and it is now the top item in run plan §10.

**Every remaining Tier A gap is a page the textbook does not cover.** With Lecture 10 done, the eight outstanding Tier A entries are exactly §4's uncovered list — all five of Lecture 7 (sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria, paraphilic disorders), both sleep-wake pages, and gambling. The list is closed, finite, and has been known since July.

**Recording a scope limit as *empty* rather than *annotated* was a deliberate call.** A section whose only content is a `> **Needs research:**` blockquote still parses as empty (`prose=false`), so it lands in `needs` — instructor work — while telling the reader exactly what is missing. Adding one token sentence of prose to each would have converted 36 instructor gaps into 36 student annotations and quietly falsified `reference_worklist`. The **one** page where the annotated form was right is `communication-disorders`, whose Presentation section has real content on social (pragmatic) communication disorder *plus* a marker naming the three communication disorders the source never mentions — a scoped ask a student can actually take. Empty sections rose 95 → 142; 36 of the 47 are this, and the jump is honest rather than a regression.

**Catalogue-first also means declining material.** Module 16 covers pica, rumination disorder, enuresis, encopresis, stereotypic movement disorder and social (pragmatic) communication disorder at length, and **none has a catalogue slug**, so none got a page. Stereotypic movement disorder and social (pragmatic) communication disorder were folded into the two new overviews and `communication-disorders` respectively, where they earn their place as differentials; the feeding and elimination disorders were left out. The check that stops a source inventing catalogue entries is the same check that stops it padding the corpus — whether the catalogue *should* gain those five rows is a separate, cheap decision, now logged as an open question.

**The hand-rolled slice became a script.** Module 13 sliced the book HTML by hand; that does not survive being done seventeen times and will not survive a second textbook. `scripts/wsu-module-extract.mjs` prints any module as markdown, `--list` prints every chapter's byte offset and size, and `WSU_BOOK_HTML` repoints it at another book. It converts every `<img>` to a visible `[[IMAGE: file]]` marker — the part not to reimplement casually, since a silently dropped figure is how Table 13.1 nearly went missing. Module 16 has **zero images**, established in one pass rather than by inspection.

**The review pass arrived early, by accident.** The post-run corpus check found a pre-existing defect: `historical-traditions` (a Module 1 pipeline page) linked to `[[abnormal-behavior]]`, which is not a catalogue slug and has no page. Retargeted to `[[what-is-abnormal]]` with `edit_page()`. **Every red link in the corpus now resolves to a real catalogue slug** — the six that remain (`suicide-and-self-harm` with 7 inbound, `brief-psychotic-disorder`, `hypersomnolence-disorder`, `kleptomania`, `pyromania`) are the designed state. That one defect is the argument for running the pass on Modules 01–12, 14 and 15 properly.

**`suicide-and-self-harm` is now the most-linked unwritten page in the corpus**, at 7 inbound references — five of them added by Module 16, where ADHD, autism, conduct disorder, specific learning disorder and intermittent explosive disorder each report suicide risk. It is the only unwritten foundation and the textbook does not cover it.

**Next is a second textbook, including a Canadian one.** Run plan §10 is the brief: the four gap classes in yield order, and the six places where a US source is not merely foreign but *wrong for the course* — duty to warn (the corpus documents `tarasoff-duty-to-warn`, a California decision, where Canadian practice runs on *Smith v Jones*), all conduct/disruptive prevalence, provincial rather than US special-education identification, CADDRA and CANMAT practice guidance, fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (absent from the WSU book entirely), and Canadian suicide statistics.

### Status / next steps

Built and **live-tested 2026-07-24** on branch `feature/academic-partition` (env vars set, staff registration + invite consumption click-tested by Norm). The plan's §5 mode-comparison test was run the same day on **four** papers spanning the layout space — Rosenhan 1973 (dense 2-col Science), Dawes/Faust/Meehl 1993 (book chapter), Young 1916 (OCR'd Internet Archive scan), Borsboom 2017 (modern 2-col with figures). Results (confirmed numbers in `ingest-budget-estimate.md` on the Academic drive): **content parity between modes on all four**; page-count differences are run-to-run concept-carving variance, not a mode effect; filenames are unstable run-to-run, so production must ingest sequentially against the accumulated index and never both modes into the production wiki; native averages ~$0.39/ingest vs extracted ~$0.27 (premium = page-image input tokens). **Decision (Norm, 2026-07-24): native is the course default** (no text-layer dependency — the robustness student submissions will exercise); the portal pre-selects it and labels it as default, with extracted kept as a cost-experiment toggle. The dual-mode test jobs were purged the same day — the four canonical **native** runs (and their PDFs) are all that remain, so the wiki index is one consistent carve per paper. Phase 2 (student submission flow, review queue, wiki publishing) designed but not built.
